#3198. Centrus' Backlog Hit $5.4 Billion. Its Quarterly Revenue Was $55 Million. Here's How Those Numbers Fit Together.

Investors shouldn't conflate its backlog with its actual revenue.

Centrus Energy (LEU +2.09%) is a linchpin of the nuclear energy market. It's one of the few U.S. companies licensed to sell low-enriched uranium (LEU), the most common fuel for conventional nuclear reactors. It's also the only publicly traded U.S. producer of high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) for next-gen nuclear reactors.

Centrus' contingent LEU and HALEU backlog swelled to $5.4 billion at the end of the third quarter of 2026, up from $3.0 billion in the second quarter. However, it only generated $55.5 million in revenue in the third quarter. In the first nine months of 2026, it generated $308.3 million in revenue, and it expects that figure to reach $450-$500 million for the full year. Let's see why there's such a huge gap between its backlog and reported revenue.

Centrus' growing backlog looks impressive, but those commitments extend through 2040. Meanwhile, its quarterly and annual revenues include only the orders it delivers, bills, and recognizes under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) within that period.

Nuclear power utilities also typically secure their supply chains years in advance through long-term contracts. So while Centrus is locking in more contracts, they won't necessarily boost its near-term revenue. Instead, analysts expect Centrus' annual revenue to grow at only a 3-year CAGR of 2.6%, from $448.7 million in 2025 to $484.5 million in 2028. They expect its net income to decline from $77.8 million in 2025 to $66.9 million in 2028.

Some major changes will also throttle Centrus' near-term growth. About 13 years ago, Centrus stopped enriching its own LEU in the U.S. after it became cheaper to import LEU from overseas and resell it to U.S. utilities. But in recent years, the sanctions against Russia and the U.S. push toward energy independence drove Centrus to restart its domestic LEU plants.

The U.S. plans to ban all Russian uranium imports by 2028, before Centrus can fully restart its domestic LEU operations or ramp up HALEU production. That's why its growth will remain sluggish over the next few years, even as the nuclear energy market expands.

With an enterprise value of $3.4 billion, Centrus might seem reasonably valued at seven times this year's sales. However, it faces more near-term challenges than many other nuclear companies that aren't undergoing massive, capital-intensive transformations. I'd keep an eye on this stock, but I wouldn't buy it before other more promising nuclear power stocks.

#3197. ElevenLabs moves beyond voice with custom models and a work app

The $22B voice AI company also launched a partner marketplace and more Nvidia computing power.

ElevenLabs co-founder and CEO Mati Staniszewski at All-In x RAISE Summit in Paris, 8 July 2026

ElevenLabs will help businesses fine-tune AI models on data from their own customer conversations, and opened early access to ElevenAI, an app that takes meeting notes. It also launched a partner programme and marketplace, and expanded its deal with Nvidia.

ElevenLabs will help businesses fine-tune AI models on data from their own customer conversations, the voice AI company announced at its New York summit on Wednesday. It also launched a workplace app, a partner programme and a marketplace.

In the coming months, firms can work with its researchers to tune its voice models and some open-source AI models. They can pick goals such as happier customers or fewer errors. The models then keep improving as more calls come in.

“Within a few years, conversational agents will become critical infrastructure for every enterprise, as essential as cloud or payments,” said CEO Mati Staniszewski.

ElevenLabs also previewed new features for ElevenAgents, its platform for voice and chat agents. Memory will let agents remember returning customers, such as one who prefers Spanish and can only talk after 5pm. Routines will handle follow-up work, such as calling back a mortgage applicant or offering a cancelled appointment to someone on a waiting list.

For staff, ElevenAI listens to meetings and turns them into notes and to-do lists. ElevenLabs says it asks for everyone’s consent before taking notes. Free early access opened on Wednesday.

It says it has more than 550 partners in 44 countries, including Google Cloud and Deloitte. It also signed a deal with McKinsey. From next year, firms can buy apps built by partners in its new marketplace.

ElevenLabs also expanded its deal with Nvidia, adding 15 MW of new computing power for large customers. The two are building a voice agent that calls patients with landlines for Poland’s national health booking system. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had been due to speak, pulled out of the event this week, as Nvidia’s board runs an inquiry into his conduct.

The push comes as ElevenLabs, valued at $22B in September with about $600M in revenue, faces cheaper rivals such as OpenAI’s voice models. Staniszewski said last week it could start preparing for an IPO in 2028.

#3196. watchOS 27.3: Three new features coming soon to Apple Watch

watchOS 27.3 will launch to all users next month and introduce these three new Apple Watch features.

Siri AI keeps getting new features and also expanding to more languages. And in watchOS 27.3, the assistant will improve in both categories.

watchOS 27.3 upgrades Siri AI with new app actions across built-in apps like Calendar, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, and Weather. With these capabilities, Siri on your wrist can do more than ever.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

Which of watchOS 27.3’s new features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

#3194. Generac: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Manufacturing is working to triple production with minimal capital spending, a structural advantage that reshapes return-on-investment expectations.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, Generac (GNRC +6.72%) announced record quarterly net sales of $1.29 billion, powered by growth in its data center backup generator business. Rapid expansion in commercial power infrastructure gives the company a multiyear revenue runway as technology operators expand artificial intelligence computing capacity.

Hyperscale cloud providers are locking in backup power supply years in advance to protect massive infrastructure investments. Generac secured a multiyear supply deal with Amazon, expanding its overall data center order pipeline.

Scaling large megawatt generator manufacturing usually requires heavy fixed-asset spending that weighs on returns. Management is expanding output through existing facilities and added assembly lines, keeping capital requirements modest relative to expected revenue.

Entry-level portable generators serve as a direct customer acquisition funnel for higher-margin home standby units. Reclaiming top market share in portable generators feeds the long-term residential upgrade pipeline.

Demand for artificial intelligence power backup is accelerating across global markets. Generac maintains structural advantages in customized packaging integration and short lead times, while management monitors factory staffing ramps and supply chain execution.

Geographic footprint expansions in Europe, Asia, and Latin America position the business for sustained international growth as commercial demand scales.

#3192. London’s Fractile raises $720M for memory-first AI chips and hits $7B valuation

London-based chip designer Fractile has raised $720 million in a Series C round, betting that memory bandwidth, rather than raw computing power, is the main constraint holding back AI performance.

The funding values the four-year-old company at $7 billion, according to the Financial Times, which cited people familiar with the deal.

Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed, and Redpoint led the round. Other investors include Alphabet’s CapitalG, DST Global, BlackRock, Bain Capital Ventures, T. Rowe Price, Shopify Ventures, Balderton, the UK’s Sovereign AI fund, and the British Business Bank.

The valuation is a sharp jump from May, when Fractile raised around $220 million at a valuation of roughly $1 billion. The new figure puts it among the UK’s most valuable startups, alongside companies such as Revolut.

The Financial Times also reports that Anthropic has expressed interest in becoming an early customer for Fractile’s chips, citing people familiar with the discussions.

Founder Walter Goodwin’s argument starts with a growing imbalance between computing power and memory bandwidth.

Over the past 25 years, chip performance has increased roughly a millionfold, while memory bandwidth has grown only about 40 times. That leaves a 25,000-fold gap between the amount of data processors can calculate and how quickly they can access it.

Goodwin told the FT that today’s frontier models are “drinking through a straw”.

Fractile’s proposed solution combines custom DRAM and logic in a three-dimensional stack. The company says this architecture can deliver substantially higher bandwidth than high-bandwidth memory (HBM), while retaining enough capacity to run large models with long context windows. Goodwin claims it could make inference, the process of generating responses to user queries, up to 10 times faster.

Those performance gains have yet to be demonstrated in a production chip. Fractile has not released a commercial product, and its first chip is planned for next year. For now, the $7 billion valuation is based on its technology and prototypes rather than a product in the market.

The company is also trying to avoid a growing constraint in the AI supply chain. Many competing chipmakers rely on HBM to move data quickly between memory and processors.

The technology is expensive, and demand from AI companies is putting pressure on suppliers such as SK Hynix and Micron.

Fractile is entering an increasingly crowded market. Nvidia acquired Groq last year and launched its own inference chip in March, while startups including Etched, MatX, and fellow British company Olix are developing alternatives.

The opportunity, according to Thrive Capital’s Philip Clark, is an inference market that could soon become “at least as large as the market Nvidia is addressing today”.

He sees particular potential in AI agents, which need to run continuously for hours or days rather than respond to a single prompt.

The funding is also a significant moment for the UK’s effort to build domestic AI infrastructure. Goodwin described the government’s Sovereign AI fund as a driving force behind developing frontier AI technology from London.

Fractile also has offices in the US and Taiwan, however, and is building for a global market. Its next challenge is to turn its prototypes into working chips that can deliver the performance it has promised.

#3190. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

New product distribution channels and higher fee rates on core strategies position the firm for revenue growth beyond near-term client shifts.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, Artisan Partners (APAM -4.28%) reported that expanding credit and alternative strategies cushioned significant equity asset outflows. Long-term investors care because client asset flows are shifting toward higher-fee private and credit strategies while core equity strategies weather temporary rebalancing.

Three key takeaways stand out for long-term investors.

Credit and alternative strategies give the firm a growth driver that moves independently from traditional stock market cycles. These strategies bring higher fee rates and attract steady institutional capital.

#3188. For Singles Day, World explains why real is the new attractive

Singles’ Day falls on 11 November each year and has become the world’s biggest online shopping event.

New Harris Poll research on behalf of World finds that 81% of singles would be more likely to use a dating app if every profile were confirmed as a real person.

As millions of singles celebrate Singles Day on November 11, the biggest question in online dating is no longer “are we compatible?” but “are you even real?”

A new survey conducted by The Harris Poll on behalf of World shows that trust has become the most important factor in online dating. Nearly 3 in 4 online daters (74%) say they have suspected that someone they matched with on a dating app was not a real person. Catfishing, AI-generated profiles, bots and romance scams have turned swiping into a guessing game, and singles say they are tired of it.

World’s answer is Proof of Human: a way for anyone to show they are a real, unique person online without revealing who they are.

The survey paints a clear picture of how much doubt singles now bring to every match:

In other words, being real now outranks looks. For a growing number of singles, authenticity is the new chemistry.

Singles are not giving up on dating apps. They are asking for proof. According to the research, 81% would be more likely to use a dating app if every profile were confirmed as belonging to a real person.

They are also willing to do their part. Four in five singles (80%) say they would take steps to prove there is a real person behind their own profile, as long as their matches did the same. Verification, in other words, is becoming a two-way expectation rather than a burden.

World ID is a universal set of human Proofs that lets people show they are a real, unique person online without sharing personal data such as their name, birthday or address. It is built for a world where AI can generate convincing faces, voices and conversations at scale.

The core of the system is the Orb, a spherical verification device. A person stands in front of it, and the Orb uses images of the eyes and face to confirm they are a unique, living human. That check is turned into an anonymous cryptographic credential, a verified World ID, stored in the World ID App. The process does not require a name, email or gender.

A few features make the technology a natural fit for dating:

The result is a simple promise for singles: the person on the other end of the chat is real.

The largest names in dating are moving in this direction. World first partnered with Match Group, the parent company of Tinder, on a World ID pilot in Japan in 2025. In April 2026, at World’s Lift Off event, the partnership expanded to the United States.

Tinder users who verify with World ID can display a human badge on their profile, signaling to potential matches that a verified, real person is behind it. Verification is optional.

Dating is only one use case. World ID is also being integrated into video calls, document signing, live event ticketing and gaming, with partners including Zoom and Docusign. The common thread is the same one singles describe in the survey: in the age of AI, knowing you are dealing with a real human is becoming essential.

The survey was conducted online in the United States by The Harris Poll on behalf of World from August 20 to 21, 2026, among 892 single adults aged 18 and over, of whom 649 have used online dating apps. Results are accurate to within +/- 3.6 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

They prioritize driving performance over everything

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve said it countless times this year: If there’s one type of vehicle I’ve driven more than anything else, it’s the 3-row family hauler. When you’re looking for maximum passenger capacity without skimping on comfort, full-size SUVs certainly fit the bill — and the Nissan Armada and Dodge Durango are no exception.

Unlike mainstream models like the Chevrolet Tahoe or GMC Yukon Denali that prioritize plush comfort over driving dynamics — often making them feel like lumbering giants — these two are far from it. Instead, these heavyweights prove that family practicality and raw enthusiasm can genuinely coexist.

The $55,225 as-tested 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition delivers pure old-school muscle with a 475-hp 6.4-liter HEMI V8 engine that sounds genuinely imposing. That looks like a steal next to the $83,735 as-tested price of the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo, but the Nismo counters with a twin-turbo V6 pushing 460 horsepower, sharper styling, and enough high-tech amenities to make a case for its steeper sticker.

After testing each one for a week, only one earns my recommendation.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

NISMO-Tuned 3.5L Twin-Turbo V6 Engine (4WD)

17 mpg city / 16 mpg highway / 19 mpg combined

13 mpg city / 19 mpg highway / 15 mpg combined

Frankly, neither design captured my attention at first — but one of them eventually grew on me. Even though they compete in the full-size, 3-row segment, they take entirely different styling routes.

The 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition leans hard into classic muscle swagger — reminiscent of the Dodge Charger — with its scooped performance hood, functional air intakes, bold Brembo brake calipers, and a rounded profile that still looks surprisingly menacing. It catches plenty of glances thanks to that aggressive stance, but it lacks the visual flair to truly sell me on its familiar look.

Between the two, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo gets my nod. Despite its noticeably more upright, boxy proportions, it delivers far more drama and curb appeal. Nissan gave it the full NISMO treatment, outfitting the SUV with massive 22-inch machined alloy wheels, an aggressive front fascia and grille, sculpted side steps with flared fenders, and full-width LED taillights. The sharp two-tone premium paint finish seals the deal, transforming this traditionally square full-size SUV into an imposing showstopper worthy of a cameo in a Fast & Furious flick.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

Nobody shops for performance-tuned, three-row SUVs with the intent of saving on fuel. However, one of these gas-guzzlers still proved friendlier at the pump over the long haul.

The 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition surprised me most on dedicated highway runs, achieving a best mark of 24.2 mpg and handily overdelivering on its 19-mpg highway rating. On short-distance trips, I averaged 21.6 mpg — equally impressive given its 13-mpg city EPA estimate. Overall, it managed 18.1 mpg across 237.9 total miles of mixed driving.

In comparison, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo made a much stronger case for real-world consistency. While its best recorded long-distance run of 23.9 mpg fell just shy of the Dodge, its twin-turbo V6 and 9-speed automatic worked far more efficiently across everyday traffic. Over the course of 302 miles of mixed driving, the Armada Nismo delivered an average of 19.9 mpg — not only beating its official 17-mpg combined EPA rating, but also comfortably edging out the Durango by nearly two full miles per gallon overall. When you’re feeding a sport-tuned hauler week in and week out, that spread makes a noticeable difference.

When SUVs are slapped with performance badges, driving dynamics are what make them special over conventional haulers. While the Armada managed to surprise me in a big way, the Durango takes the crown here.

Nissan deserves immense credit for defying expectations given the Armada's boxy proportions, which initially made me apprehensive about driving it on crowded highways. It packs a genuinely strong 3.5-liter twin-turbo V6 pushing 460 horsepower and 516 lb-ft of torque, delivering instant thrust and effortless passing power.

It's also surprisingly easy to drive for its size, thanks to an ultra-responsive steering wheel that feels very light and loose. If that’s not enough, its adaptive electronic air suspension and great shocks make cruising over bumpy roads a breeze.

Yet for all the Armada’s composure, it can’t match the raw power and exhilarating feel of the 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 Launch Edition. Backed by a 475-horsepower 6.4-liter HEMI V8 under the hood, it completely transforms the driving experience.

Between the thunderous exhaust roar, immediate throttle response, and quick Brembo stopping power, the Durango delivers a far more thrilling ride every time I put the pedal to the metal. Honestly, it handles like a muscle car — giving enthusiasts the genuine excitement that almost every other three-row hauler lacks.

Both SUVs deliver great accommodations when it comes to passenger capacity, but one takes interior luxury and space to another level. What I love about both full-size haulers is how they offer second-row captain's chairs paired with a convenient center console for cupholders and armrest storage.

In the Dodge Durango R/T 392, second-row passengers have 38.6 inches of legroom to stretch out comfortably, while the third-row bench yields 33.5 inches. Even though adults can fit back there, my knees practically touch the seatbacks in front of me. Finally, there’s a cavernous 17.2 cubic feet of cargo space behind the third row that easily swallowed my electric scooter without needing to wedge it at an angle.

The one big downside for the Durango is that it lacks lane-centering assist when adaptive cruise control is engaged — meaning, it won't actively keep you centered between the lines.

The 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo simply offers more cabin volume to comfortably seat adults while pampering them with genuine luxury. Thanks to its taller cabin, legroom feels far more generous in the second row with 39.2 inches of space, while the third row provides 32.9 inches. The Armada also delivers significantly more cargo capacity behind the rear seats with 20.4 cubic feet of trunk space.

Between its plush, red-and-black trimmed NISMO suede seats, whisper-quiet cabin insulation, and ProPILOT Assist for hands-free highway cruising, the Armada makes long distance drices effortless no matter where you sit. That said, its lane centering isn't always spot-on when activated, but the overall luxury leap is impossible to ignore.

On paper, the pricing advantage leans heavily toward the Durango, but it's important to look at what each model actually delivers before jumping to conclusions.

Dodge’s value proposition is centered squarely on performance, yet this bargain full-size SUV still includes a respectable set of amenities. For example, you get a single-pane sunroof, a Harman Kardon sound system, and a standard backup camera. Still, I’m not as impressed with the dashboard layout, which leans far too conventional and dated.

By contrast, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo commands a steep $83,735 as-tested price that’s nearly $28,500 higher than its rival. That’s a significant stretch, but it buys a modern suite of luxury and tech features: an expansive panoramic moonroof, a high-fidelity 12-speaker Klipsch premium audio system, heated front seats, and a sophisticated 3D Enhanced Intelligent Around View Monitor that makes navigating tight parking spaces a breeze.

While the Armada undoubtedly delivers the more modern, tech-rich experience, the Durango's $55,225 as-tested price makes it an untouchable performance bargain in the three-row space.

I can’t overstate the price disparity between these two sport-tuned SUVs, with one costing nearly $28,500 more than the other. At their core, however, both deliver large family-hauling utility without forcing you to completely give up your passion for driving.

Without question, the 2026 Nissan Armada Nismo is the superior all-around modern SUV for everyday living. Between its sharp two-tone finish, plush suede seats, massive passenger volume, whisper-quiet cabin, and cutting-edge tech suite, it feels every bit like an $84,000 flagship that justifies its price tag. If your budget allows, the Armada won't disappoint with its effortless acceleration and smooth, composed ride — making it tough to beat.

2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition

Yet when it comes to the vehicle I’d actually spend my own money on, the 2026 Dodge Durango R/T 392 AWD Launch Edition gets my vote, despite coming up short on paper once all the category scores are tallied. Sure, the Durango's interior aesthetics lack the modern flair of its rival, but it unapologetically prioritizes genuine muscle car performance with three rows of seats.

With an as-tested price of $55,225, it isn’t just competitive — it's an untouchable performance bargain in a segment otherwise dominated by $60K+ land yachts.

#3184. Why training alone can’t close the gap between AI adoption and ROI

You’re likely familiar with some version of this narrative: companies adopt AI, performance gains eventually plateau, and leaders are left wondering about the ROI from their investments.

Experts disagree on how to remedy this gap between adoption and results. Some call for better governance, others for better deployment. Or my personal favorite, better enablement. Each one of these remedies depends upon organizations being aligned on what success looks like and being able to measure it.

Take learning and development (L&D) professionals. They may be supporting your AI adoption plans while facing the same organizational issues. That’s right, the people most prepared to build skills are also struggling to measure the ROI of AI.

We surveyed more than 800 workplace learning professionals across more than 25 countries for our annual AI in Learning & Development Report. Here’s what we can learn from them about getting from adoption to results.

How L&D teams use AI reflects what their organization rewards and measures.

If employees are working at organizations that track AI usage and reward more tokens being used, then teams’ AI use will reflect that. This type of reward only becomes an issue when it isn’t paired with clear measurement outcomes. Organizations need to be able to say, we want you to use more AI, in order to accomplish X. Otherwise, they’re left with productivity gains that amount to little performance improvement.

In our report, 75% of respondents named faster content creation as one of the clearest impacts they’ve seen from AI adoption. This looks like reducing the time it takes to produce new training and increasing the output of training. Meanwhile, only 11% named improved on-the-job performance as an impact.

Most workplace training is designed to improve on-the-job performance. Yet only 35% of L&D teams are consistently measuring that (compared to 72% who consistently measure participation and completions).

This suggests that leaders are either rewarding and measuring L&D performance against those metrics, or that no one has agreed on what success should look like. Our survey responses point to the latter. More than one in five name a lack of agreed-upon success metrics as their biggest barrier to proving impact.

Rewards aren’t the only organizational constraint L&D teams face when they adopt AI. What an organization permits, how it governs AI, matters just as much.

That starts with which AI solutions teams can access. 73% of L&D teams that started from a leadership mandate to use AI still need departmental or cross-functional permission to pilot a new AI tool. Some teams are limited to company-approved AI tools and can’t test beyond that.

Teams also need the right data to evaluate AI’s impact. A majority of L&D teams are confident that AI is leading to improvements, but struggle to provide evidence of those gains. Asked for the biggest barrier to proving impact, 53% pointed to an organizational constraint, including the lack of agreed-upon success metrics and access to data or measurement tools.

That might look like data needed to measure impact living in disconnected systems, such as a Learning Management System, an HR Information System, a survey tool, and an AI video platform.

If L&D teams are using AI to churn out training faster, but aren’t evaluating whether that training is leading to behavioral change, then they’re just using AI as a content factory. Until leaders agree on outcomes beyond speed, more content is all those teams will have to show for AI adoption.

The good news is that about a third of L&D teams report performance gains from AI, like faster time to proficiency or improved on-the-job performance. Several traits set these teams apart, like being able to freely pilot or build AI solutions, or using AI to evaluate their work. Those factors often depend on organizational factors beyond L&D’s control.

Based on our data, there are three structural changes leaders can make to their AI strategy to deliver ROI.

First, align on what AI is supposed to accomplish, then on how its usage is rewarded and measured. Without a defined outcome, teams produce what’s easiest to show, which in L&D is faster content. For L&D teams, that means working with leaders to identify the performance changes they want to see, and how to measure them, before designing any new training. And yes, that includes AI enablement.

Second, invest in data integration before scaling new AI solutions or automating more workflows. Make sure teams across functions have access to the data they need to measure AI’s impact.

Third, partner with L&D on your AI strategy. If the goal of AI is to automate manual work, then the goal should be to free up time for more strategic capability building, like how to use AI to change how work gets done. L&D is well suited to lead that capability building because they can identify where training can be part of the solution and where it can’t.

Only then can training help close the gap between AI adoption and ROI.

#3183. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

#3182. CTO Realty: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Acquisitions below replacement cost and double-digit structured yields show how CTO is working to extract value beyond traditional leasing.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 28, 2026, CTO Realty (CTO +0.10%) announced that it raised its full-year guidance after deploying $472 million into investments. For retail real estate investors, cash flow growth hinges on filling vacant spaces quickly and putting capital into high-yielding properties. The company's execution shows how active asset management turns vacant storefronts into durable rental income.

Three key takeaways from the call highlight its trajectory.

When major retail tenants close, landlords lose both rent and foot traffic. Management eliminated that drag by resolving all 11 vacated anchor spaces in its portfolio. It achieved a 70% cash-rent spread, which measures the percentage increase between previous and new lease rates.

CTO Realty entered the Kansas City market by purchasing Zona Rosa, an open-air shopping destination, for $63 million. Management bought the property at foreclosure for $82 per square foot. That is well below replacement cost, giving the company a clear path to boost earnings as it fills vacant space.

Beyond physical real estate, the company deploys capital into high-yield loans and preferred equity, which gives priority over common equity for dividends and asset recovery. These structured deals generate double-digit yields without requiring full asset ownership.

Leasing demand across the retail portfolio is expanding steadily, supported by consistent tenant interest and below-market rents. CTO Realty benefits from long-term leases with creditworthy anchors and a new $1 billion credit facility, which provides access to flexible corporate debt, lowers borrowing costs, and extends debt maturities.

Management is focusing on capital allocation, executing its signed-not-open pipeline, and unlocking value from newly acquired lifestyle centers. The company relies on its embedded growth drivers to fuel long-term shareholder returns.

#3181. Apple reportedly met with Thai officials over spyware alerts sent to politicians

Bloomberg reports that Apple has met with Thai government officials in the wake of its recent wave of iPhone alerts about mercenary spyware attacks. Here are the details.

Last week, The Financial Times and TechCrunch reported that Apple had sent a fresh wave of threat notifications to potential spyware targets in 99 countries, warning them that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks.

At the time, the FT focused on German lawmakers who had received the warnings, while TechCrunch highlighted recipients in other countries, including Beirut-based filmmaker Radwan Mortada.

Today, Bloomberg reported that “Thailand held meetings with Apple Inc. officials” over the notifications, adding that the warnings raised questions about “who may have targeted [Thai politicians] and why.”

Receiving an alert doesn’t necessarily mean a device was successfully compromised, Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob said after meeting Apple representatives Wednesday, Krungthep Turakij and other media reported. Thai authorities also have no evidence so far that the latest attempted attacks involved Pegasus, the spyware developed by Israel’s NSO Group, he said.

As Bloomberg explains, Pegasus was “allegedly used against pro-democracy campaigners in 2022.”

The recent wave of alerts, which were sent out on October 29, followed another round in August, when Apple notified potential targets in 110 countries. As always, Apple declined to disclose what triggers these notifications to prevent attackers from evading detection in the future, but recommended that recipients enable Lockdown Mode and seek expert security assistance.

Bloomberg added that Thai authorities are expected to meet with other technology companies on Thursday to discuss potential countermeasures, including risks to Android devices.

#3179. Stock Market Today, Nov. 11: Nvidia Rebounds as CoreWeave Earnings Reignite the AI Trade

Nvidia and other semiconductor stocks rallied Wednesday as CoreWeave's latest earnings reinforced demand for AI infrastructure, helping Wall Street recover from Tuesday's sell-off.

Nvidia (NVDA +2.87%), the leading manufacturer of artificial intelligence (AI) chips and data center computing systems, rebounded 2.87% on Wednesday, November 11, closing at $173.73 as strong earnings from CoreWeave (CRWV +24.71%) helped restore confidence in the AI trade. The rally followed Tuesday's steep sell-off, with investors finding renewed optimism in CoreWeave's surging revenue and growing demand for AI infrastructure.

Trading volume reached 266.6 million shares, more than double its three-month daily average of 129.6 million, underscoring strong investor interest in the rebound. With Nvidia scheduled to report earnings on November 17, attention is turning to whether the chipmaker can sustain its growth momentum amid ongoing concerns about China restrictions and uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang.

Wall Street rebounded sharply on Wednesday, with technology stocks leading the recovery following Tuesday's inflation-driven sell-off. The S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.31%) climbed 1.29% to 7,618, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.60%) advanced 1.60% to 25,466.

Semiconductor stocks were among the session's strongest performers, with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +7.32%) surging 7.32% to $552.90 and Broadcom (AVGO +3.99%) gaining 3.99% to $345.22. Both outperformed Nvidia, suggesting the rally extended beyond a single company as investors regained confidence in the broader AI industry.

Wednesday's rebound suggests investors remain confident in the long-term outlook for AI infrastructure, despite recent volatility. CoreWeave's stronger-than-expected results and improved revenue guidance provide encouraging evidence that demand for computing capacity continues to outpace available supply. As a major supplier of the GPUs powering these data centers, Nvidia stands to benefit from sustained infrastructure investment.

However, the rally doesn't eliminate the risks facing Nvidia. Baird downgraded the stock to Neutral on Wednesday, citing uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang, potential restrictions on chip exports to China, and slowing growth in hyperscaler capital expenditures heading into 2027. These concerns could weigh on Nvidia's valuation even if near-term demand remains strong.

Nvidia's November 17 earnings report will provide a critical test of its growth outlook. Investors should focus on data center revenue, profit margins, and management's forward guidance, particularly whether demand for next-generation chips remains strong enough to offset potential weakness in China. Strong results could help sustain the recovery, but longer-term confidence will also depend on greater clarity surrounding Huang's leadership and the regulatory outlook.

#3178. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

Crypto exchange Binance has warned iPhone users about an iOS vulnerability that could allow malicious apps to access sensitive data stored by other apps. Here are the details.

In a post published on X (via AppleInsider), Binance says that a vulnerability called worse_query could allow “malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem.”

Binance says the flaw affects iOS 26.7.1, iOS 27.0.1, and iOS 27.2. However, a Community Note points out that researchers describe the vulnerability as an unpatched zero-day and that Apple’s latest security updates, including iOS 27.2.1 (the current version at the time of writing), do not mention a fix.

A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.…

That said, in addition to updating their devices, Binance recommends that iPhone crypto holders take the following immediate actions:

The vulnerability was disclosed by security researchers @0xjohnny and @forcequitOS, who published a proof of concept on GitHub demonstrating how it can be used to bypass iOS sandbox protections, which normally prevent apps from accessing each other’s files.

Researcher @forcequitOS also noted that neither iOS 27.2.1 nor iOS 27.3 beta 1 patches the vulnerability.

Just as a general statement so there isn’t any confusion about it, worse_query is *not* patched in iOS 27.2.1 and 27.3 beta 1. I’ll update version support on the readme when it’s patched.

Although the researcher describes the code as intended for developers and not useful on its own, other developers have already built apps using it, including a file manager that can access, modify, and delete data belonging to other apps without requiring a jailbreak.

According to The Hacker News, neither Binance nor the researchers have reported any attacks or cryptocurrency thefts involving the vulnerability so far.

#3173. iPhone Duo one week later: The future, or not for me?

My iPhone Duo arrived last Thursday, so I’ve had a week to use it as my daily carry. My early experience has been mixed, so I keep asking myself an important question: is this the iPhone’s future and I just need to adapt, or is the Duo simply not for everyone?

After a week using the iPhone Duo, in some ways I have a lot of clarity about the product, and in other ways my thinking is very clouded.

To put it simply: I’m not having a great time with the Duo, which makes me wonder if the problem is me, not it.

I’ve seen countless social media posts from Duo owners proclaiming how much they love the product. And I absolutely believe them. The iPhone Duo is a remarkable innovation for the iPhone. It’s cool, weird, and wonderful in all sorts of ways. But for me and my needs (preferences?), it’s been more frustrating than enjoyable.

And that frustration mainly boils down to one thing: I almost never want to open it.

I’d estimate at least 90% of my iPhone Duo usage involves the front display. And when I unfold it the remaining 10% of the time, it’s often because I force myself to do it in the hopes of discovering what I’m missing out on. Like, I know I should be unfolding it more, so I do. But it doesn’t add any real value for me.

Because I rarely want to open the iPhone Duo, I’m left using the outer display all the time. In that mode, the Duo is too heavy for extended use, too wide to comfortably reach, and the UI in most apps is an adjustment.

Are these dealbreakers? No. I could live with the Duo’s outer display if I had to, but it’s definitely an inferior experience to my iPhone 18 Pro.

If I was opening the iPhone Duo more, and actually taking advantage of the key value proposition of foldables—that you can unfold them—I doubt the outer screen would bother me much.

But what I’ve found, at least so far, is that one-handed iPhone use is very important to me, which rules out using the inner display. I use my iPhone mostly for quick interactions, and often with a child in one hand (I have three very young kids). In situations when I do have two hands free to open the Duo, I’m probably sitting in front of my iPad Pro with a Magic Keyboard attached and would rather use the iPad instead.

So again: is the problem with the Duo, or with me?

My colleague seems to like it but he struggles a bit with the case and the folded screen.

I forgot to add, that he has the Apple case for the phone.

I think it’s the latter, but I’m not sure “problem” is the right word. I just don’t find myself using it the way it’s meant to be used. And that’s fine.

I want to love the iPhone Duo, because I see how much fun other people are having with it. And maybe given more time, something will click and I’ll start to use it “as intended.”

If iPhone Duo is the future of the iPhone, I’ll adapt and move on with my life. But one week in, I think it’s probably just not for me. And if it’s not for me, maybe there are a lot of people who will continue preferring non-foldable iPhones for many years to come.

What’s your iPhone Duo experience been like? Are you loving it or struggling? Let us know in the comments.

These could be the reasons for your leaf blower malfunction

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If, like me, your lawn is completely covered with fallen leaves, a leaf blower is a must-have garden tool. Not only can they quickly make cleanup a breeze (no pun intended), but they can also save you the back-breaking task of raking up piles of leaves.

So when your reliable leaf blower keeps cutting out unexpectedly right in the middle of a task, this can be frustrating. Rest assured, you are not the only one dealing with this frequent issue.

In fact, all it takes is a few quick checks and troubleshooting steps that will keep your leaf blower running reliably and ensure your lawn stays free of leaves all season. Here's what you need to do when your leaf blower suddenly stops running.

The first thing is to check for clogs, which will only take minutes. Clogging from trapped debris is a common reason both gas- and electric-powered leaf blowers cut out, as it restricts essential airflow.

For gas leaf blowers, simply remove the filter cover and give it a good clean before taking out the filter itself. To clean it, clear away any loose dirt or debris, then use compressed air to blast out any stubborn blockages.

For electric leaf blowers, simply remove debris in the air intake vent and give it a good wipe-down. Once you’ve done that, this should resolve the annoying shut-off issues you have.

If you have a gas-powered leaf blower, your gasoline might be the culprit of blockages that can affect the engine. This is usually the case if you haven’t used your blower for a long time, and the bad gasoline is no longer fit for use.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Fortunately, this is an easy fix — simply drain the old gasoline in a suitable container, install a new fuel filter before refilling it with fresh gas and oil mix. If the problem continues, inspect the carburetor for build-up and spray it clean with a specialized carburetor cleaner. It’s also worth checking the spark arrestor and fuel cap to remove any debris or stubborn grime.

Another top tip is to test the fuel cap to check if it needs replacing. To determine whether the fuel cap requires this, try loosening it slightly and operating the blower. If the machine runs properly while loose but stalls again once the cap is tightened back down, then a new cap is needed.

If you have a battery-powered blower, you may be dealing with a damaged battery. Usually, a faulty battery struggles to keep its proper charge, resulting in your leaf blower constantly cutting out.

Simply swap it out with a spare or new battery to see if this makes a difference to your performance.

Additionally, store your batteries properly in a dry, moisture-free location away from extreme temperatures.

#3170. Alpine Linux and OpenSSH patch flaw that’s as bad as it can get

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

This dangerous Linux security hole must be patched as soon as possible.

The perfect nightmare scenario for a Linux server is when all an attacker needs to do is reach the server’s Secure Shell (SSH) port, waltz right in, and take it over. That’s what happened to Alpine Linux, the popular, lightweight Linux server. Adding insult to injury, this happened only days after Alpine Linux dodged a security hole-sized bullet to its GitLab implementation.

Also: Linux Mint 27 arrives next month, and I like it already: What to expect

How bad is it? As bad as it can get. Alpine Linux explained in its security advisory that if an attacker can reach a vulnerable server’s SSH port, they can get in “with one connection,” and the attack “works every time, and needs no retries.”

As security engineer Gregory Bryant explained in his LinkedIn post:

Most authentication bypasses come from complex logic chains, but yesterday’s Alpine Linux OpenSSH vulnerability (CVE-2026-123158) comes down to a single character: *.”

If you run Alpine Linux (or another musl-based distro) with the default openssh-server package (no Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)) and PasswordAuthentication enabled, an attacker can log into password-disabled, or key-only accounts simply by sending a password between 257 and 1024 bytes long.

Alpine Linux isn’t the only operating system that uses musl, a lightweight version of the standard C library (libc). Other operating systems that use musl and are potentially vulnerable include Adélie Linux; Void Linux; Sabotage Linux; OpenWrt, an Android variant,  and the Yocto Project, which is used to build embedded Linux distributions.

Also: This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise

Wind River, which produces the commercial embedded Linux distro, Wind River Linux, is also looking into the issue. A company representative told me, “Wind River takes security seriously. We are actively reviewing the reported vulnerability and assessing its potential impact. We will take appropriate action as needed.”

Behind the scenes, when OpenSSH is built without PAM, it verifies passwords by hashing the password attempt using the C library’s crypt() function. It then compares the result to the account’s stored password field. So far, so good.

But when a key is longer than 256 bytes, musl’s crypt() function returns the string * as an error indicator. That is also what the password field holds for any account with no password, such as a key-only account. Thus, the “hash” matches and the login succeeds, and the attacker walks in.

Also: The new Cutefish Linux distro might be the best MacOS clone around

To exploit it, an attacker only needs the name of such an account. The attacker also needs at least one other account on the machine with a 5 or 6 password hash, and then to send a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes. According to Alpine, one user with a password is enough to make every passwordless account accessible.

In Linux systems that use glibc’s crypt(), which is almost all of them, the same attempt would return NULL on error, which sshd already rejects, so Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, etc., aren’t affected.

According to *sshole, the group that uncovered the problem, this is a side effect that has been hiding since 2016.

Alpine said every release it checked is affected: 3.21 through 3.24, edge, and the older 3.16 to 3.20 branches. Exposure requires the following:

Root is not directly exposed in most cases. It has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password blocks it. Another account that can become root, for example through doas, still gives an attacker a route to root.

Alpine singled out its official tiny-cloud images, versions 3.18.11 through 3.24.3, as especially vulnerable. These ship with an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot but become exploitable once any 6 hash exists on the machine. That can happen when an administrator sets a console password or when user data adds a user with a hashed password, which means, essentially, all of them.

Alpine released 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 on Thursday, with the OpenSSH fix among the security changes. It also published fixed packages for each release back to 3.16. Alpine 3.21 reached end of support on Nov. 1.

The just-released OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. Alpine’s stable branches carry a patch for the same problem. You should run apk upgrade -U -a and then restart the daemon with rc-service sshd restart. Alpine stressed that upgrading the package does not replace the running daemon. Anyone who cannot update should set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, after confirming that key login works.

Also: Maze Linux is the best security-focused distro I’ve ever tested

To check for an attack, Alpine told administrators to search /var/log/messages for “Accepted password for” lines that name an account with no password. It also advised reviewing dedicated OpenBSD application subexecutor (doas) use and recently created users, files, and authorized keys. “If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.” Just what you wanted for your weekend, I know, but here we are.

#3169. Oracle Stock Just Surged After CoreWeave Earnings. Here's Why One Analyst Says It's Built for the Data-Center Backlash

Oracle shares rallied with other AI stocks on Wednesday. One analyst thinks Oracle is better positioned than rivals as political pushback against data centers grows.

Oracle (ORCL +8.81%) shares rose nearly 9% to about $128 on Wednesday, part of a broad rally in AI stocks after AI cloud company CoreWeave (CRWV +24.71%) raised its revenue forecast and reported a massive order backlog of about $132.5 billion.

The jump follows a brutal stretch. Even after Wednesday's gain, Oracle is still down about 34% this year and more than 60% from its record levels last year.

CoreWeave and Oracle are in the same business: renting out huge amounts of AI computing power. Both are spending heavily to build data centers, and investors have worried about how they'll pay for it.

CoreWeave's report eased some of that worry. Its CEO, Michael Intrator, said the company's growth is funded partly by "financing backed by customer contracts" and about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone. In other words, customers are paying up front for capacity they want, which suggests demand for AI computing is real rather than speculative.

That obviously matters for Oracle, which is making the same kind of bet, but on a much bigger scale.

The latest worry for AI stocks is political. After last week's midterm elections, investors grew concerned that states and towns could restrict new data center construction. The restrictions have gotten bipartisan support. On Wednesday, Sen. Josh Hawley called for a moratorium on building them.

Still, analysts at Mizuho think Oracle is better prepared than most. In a note on Monday, the firm said all five of Oracle's mega sites are already under construction, and four have the necessary permits. The firm said potential delays are already built into Oracle's guidance, and that tighter permitting could even help Oracle by limiting new AI computing supply. Mizuho called the recent sell-off a buying opportunity and kept its Outperform rating.

Oracle's own numbers show why investors care. In its latest quarterly report, for the three months ended Aug. 31, cloud infrastructure revenue more than doubled to $7.4 billion. Total revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion.

Its remaining performance obligations, or revenue it's already under contract to collect, reached $664 billion, up from $455 billion a year earlier. Oracle said the jump came mainly from "significant" (or, large) cloud contracts.

Building all that capacity costs a fortune. Oracle spent $28.5 billion on capital expenditures in the quarter, more than three times the year before. That left free cash flow at negative $5.4 billion, well below negative $362 million one year prior. To help pay for it, Oracle raised about $19.9 billion by selling new shares, which, of course, dilutes existing shareholders.

Oracle is also carrying a lot of debt. It had about $125 billion in senior notes and other long-term borrowings at the end of August. There is a bright spot: like CoreWeave, Oracle's customers are paying in advance. Prepayments added about $11.4 billion to its operating cash flow in the quarter, helping that figure nearly triple to $23.1 billion. Profit is growing, too, with earnings per share up 54% to $1.56.

Oracle also expects to recognize only about 13% of that $664 billion over the next 12 months. Much of the payoff seems years away, and depends on customers following through.

Mizuho makes a good point: if building new data centers gets harder, companies with sites already underway have an edge. But Oracle is a high-stakes bet that AI demand will last for years.

At about $128 a share, Oracle is worth roughly $390 billion. For investors who believe in that story, the stock's 34% drop this year offers a better entry point. Just size the position for the risk, and watch Oracle's next earnings report in December for updates on spending and its backlog.
