Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users would likely start paying for some features they've long enjoyed for free.

Samsung is reportedly planning a shift from free unlimited Galaxy AI tools to a tiered subscription plan. This would be a major adjustment for Galaxy device owners who are heavy AI users, as they’d likely have to pay for some features they’ve long enjoyed for free.

Also: 7 Samsung Galaxy settings I always change

Tools like Photo Assist, Now Brief, and Creative Studio will still remain free, according to reports — they just won’t offer unlimited usage. Once the allotted number of free credits runs out, Samsung plans to introduce either standalone packages to top up AI credits or a monthly or annual subscription for users to continue using these features.

No free usage limit has been specified for users, but the highest-tiered subscription claims to offer usage limits four times higher than the free plan. A subscription would also give users access to exclusive features, presumably high-compute and newer processes.

The Galaxy AI Premium subscription would start at $4.99 per month or $47.99 per year, and reports indicate it would go up from there.

Samsung is planning to roll out a paid subscription model for the Galaxy S27 series, according to code references in 2027 Samsung devices. The company is reportedly planning to expand the plan to older devices through One UI updates, including S24 series models and newer devices, as well as Fold and Flip series phones.

If you’re an occasional Galaxy AI user, you probably won’t ever need to pay to use your preferred AI features. This would include those who edit a photo or summarize an email every now and then.

Power users and those who rely heavily on Galaxy AI daily will need to decide whether yet another subscription is worth the money. Aside from a higher token limit, these features would include AI-generated videos, Bixby Action, and Daily Briefing.

Samsung hasn’t announced a release date for the Galaxy S27 Series phones, but the company typically holds a Galaxy Unpacked event in January or February.

#3166. PolyPid (PYPD) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

FDA labeling talks are underway ahead of the D-PLEX100 review deadline, with a potential U.S. launch in view.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

PolyPid Ltd. (PYPD +4.60%) is moving toward a potential U.S. commercial launch of its lead product candidate, D-PLEX100, following the acceptance of its New Drug Application and the establishment of a strategic partnership with Azurity Pharmaceuticals. Management reported that the company is currently engaged in labeling discussions with the FDA ahead of the Nov. 28, 2026, PDUFA date. The company also regained full commercial rights for the European market and is pursuing label expansion into broader abdominal surgeries while advancing its clinical pipeline with PD01B for diabetic foot infections. Financial results for the third quarter showed a decrease in net loss and a cash position supported by milestone payments from its U.S. partner.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the PolyPid third quarter 2026 conference call. As a reminder, this call is being recorded. I would now like to introduce your host for today's conference, Yehuda Leibler from ARX Investor Relations. Mr. Leibler, you may begin.

Yehuda Leibler: Thank you, operator. Thank you all for joining PolyPid's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Earlier today, PolyPid released its financial results for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026. A copy of the press release is available on the investor section of the company's website at www.polypid.com. Joining me on the call today are Dikla Czaczkes Akselbrad, Chief Executive Officer of PolyPid, Ori Warshavsky, Chief Operating Officer U.S. of PolyPid, and Jonny Missulawin, Chief Financial Officer of PolyPid. I'd like to remind you that on this call, management will make forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws.

These include statements about the FDA's review of the D-PLEX100 NDA, including labeling discussions, the PDUFA goal date, and the FDA pre-approval inspection. They also cover the potential approval of D-PLEX100 and the anticipated timing of its U.S. commercial launch by Azurity Pharmaceuticals, as well as potential reimbursement for D-PLEX100, including the anticipated timing of a CMS decision on a New Technology Add-on Payment, or NTAP. We will also discuss the potential label expansion of D-PLEX100 and planned communications with the FDA and the EMA's review of the MAA for D-PLEX100, including the anticipated timing of the decision and a potential U.S. launch.

In addition, we will refer to the company's plans for Europe, Canada, and other territories, including potential partnerships and their timing. Finally, these statements include the company's PolyPid 2030 vision and levers for growth, the development plans and anticipated timing for PD01B and PD03A, and the company's expectation that its cash resources will be sufficient to fund operations into 2028 and through several significant upcoming potential milestones. Forward-looking statements are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, many of which are beyond the company's control, including the risks described from time to time in the company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Accordingly, you should not place undue reliance on these statements.

I encourage you to review the company's filings with the SEC, including its annual report on Form 20-F, filed on February 25, 2026. PolyPid disclaims any intention or obligation, except as required by law, to update or revise any forward-looking statements. This conference call contains time-sensitive information that speaks only as of the live broadcast today, November 11, 2026. With that, it's my pleasure to turn the call over to Dikla Czaczkes Akselbrad, Chief Executive Officer of PolyPid. Dikla?

Dikla Akselbrad: Thank you, Yehuda, and good morning, everyone. We are now just over two weeks from our PDUFA goal date of November 28th, and this is a defining moment for PolyPid. Let me start with the FDA review. Our NDA for D-PLEX100 for the prevention of surgical site infection in patients undergoing colorectal surgery is under priority review. Since the NDA was accepted in July, we have continued to work closely with the agency. Labeling discussions are underway, and all scheduled FDA interactions are on track and aligned with the PDUFA goal date. As is standard practice, we will not discuss the content of the label ahead of an approval decision.

In parallel, PolyPid and Azurity are preparing for the U.S. launch of D-PLEX100 in early 2027, subject to FDA approval, and Ori will walk you through that work. The partnership has already delivered $30 million to PolyPid, and NTAP application for D-PLEX100 has also been submitted to CMS, with a decision expected in August 2027. If granted, NTAP would provide additional reimbursement to hospital of up to 75% of the product cost above the standard DRG payment. Surgical site infections are not only a colorectal problem, and label expansion is a key growth driver for D-PLEX100.

Together with Azurity, our first step is broader abdominal surgery, including GI procedures and hysterectomies, approximately 4 million surgeries a year in the U.S. according to IQVIA. Close to half of them are open procedures. We plan to initiate communications with the FDA on this work in the fourth quarter. Beyond abdominal surgery, we see opportunities in soft tissue and bone surgery. Under our current agreement with Azurity will fund the clinical development once we jointly prioritize indications. In Europe, we submitted our marketing authorization application to the EMA on September 14, meeting the third quarter timeline we had communicated.

Shortly after quarter end, the EMA validated the application and began its formal review, with a decision expected in the second half of 2027 and a potential EU launch in 2028. At the same time, we mutually agreed with ADVANZ PHARMA to terminate our 2022 agreement for Europe, and the exclusive European commercialization rights to D-PLEX100 have revert back to us. We now fully control our European strategy, and we are in active discussions with potential commercial partners. In Canada, part of the Azurity collaboration, a new drug submission is planned for 2027.

At our investor days two weeks ago, we laid out the vision for PolyPid 2030 and our three levers of growth: maximizing D-PLEX100 through Azurity, including label expansion beyond colorectal surgery, taking D-PLEX100 into new territories, starting with Europe, and expanding our Kynatrix pipeline, beginning with PD01B for the treatment of moderate to severe diabetic foot infections, or DFI. D-PLEX100 was always meant to be our first product, not our only one.

To summarize the milestone ahead, our PDUFA goal date in two weeks' time on November 28th, the start of FDA communications on broader abdominal surgery this quarter, the U.S. launch of D-PLEX100 in early 2027, subject to approval, the NTAP decision in August 2027, and in the second half of 2027, the EMA decision, as well as the PD01B pre-IND meeting and first-in-human study. With a committed U.S. partner preparing for launch, full commercialization rights for Europe, a growing pipeline, and a strong balance sheet, we believe PolyPid is well-positioned for this next stage. With that, I will turn the call over to Ori. Ori?

Ori Warshavsky: Thank you, Dikla. I will cover our launch preparation with Azurity, new D-PLEX100 data, and our pipeline. Azurity is an established specialty pharmaceutical company with more than 70 medicines across 11 therapeutic areas, and we believe it is the right partner for D-PLEX100. It brings reach, more than 10 hospital-administered products, more than 200 U.S. commercial-facing colleagues, and the GPO contracting and institutional relationships that reach more than 1,700 leading U.S. hospitals and academic centers. It also brings relevance, a hospital-prescribed antibiotic on the market that gives it credibility with infectious disease specialists and bowel preparation products used by the same colorectal surgeons D-PLEX100 will initially serve. And it brings commitment to invest in and expand the product over time.

Since we signed the agreement in July 2026, the work has moved from planning to execution. Azurity is building out its sales force, national accounts, market access, and medical affairs team, and our companies meet in joint forums across medical, regulatory, supply chain, and commercial functions. We see the commercial launch of D-PLEX100 as a process that will build over several months, starting in early 2027. Subject to approval, Azurity's medical teams will start working with target hospitals, engaging surgeons and infectious disease specialists who can bring D-PLEX100 to the hospital's Pharmacy and Therapeutics, or P&T, committee for review and addition to formulary.

Each hospital reviews new products on their own schedule, so access will grow account by account over several months. After the quarter, we also presented D-PLEX100 microbiology data at the IDWeek 2026 conference. In a late-breaking oral presentation by Dr. George Viola of MD Anderson Cancer Center, an exploratory pooled microbiology analysis of our clinical data covering 2,185 patients looked at infections that occurred despite prevention. The finding from the abstract added microbiologic context to the SHIELD II results. Finally, we introduced PD01B for the treatment of moderate to severe diabetic foot infections at our recent R&D Day. It is our first step in extending Kynatrix from preventing infections to treating them.

Diabetic foot infections are among the most serious and costly complications of diabetes, and current treatment relies on debridement and systemic antibiotics, which can struggle to reach adequate concentration in the infected tissue with poor blood supply. PD01B is designed to be applied directly into the wound and to sustain hyper-localized, high doxycycline levels in the infected tissue over weeks. It builds on the same active ingredient, manufacturing site, and established safety database of D-PLEX100, and PolyPid holds worldwide commercial rights for it. We expect to hold a pre-IND meeting with the FDA and begin a first-in-human study in the second half of 2027. Our long-acting obesity program, PD03A, continues in early preclinical development.

With that, I will turn the call over to Jonny to review our financial results. Jonny?

Jonny Missulawin: Thank you, Ori. I will now review our financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. Research and development expenses for the third quarter of 2026 were $6.5 million compared to $5.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. The increase was primarily due to ongoing NDA-related activities and continued commercial readiness preparation. General and administrative expenses were $1.5 million compared to $1.8 million in the prior year period. The decrease was primarily due to lower non-cash expenses related to performance-based options following the positive phase III SHIELD II top-line results, which triggered the vesting of those options. Marketing and business development expenses were $0.4 million, in line with the prior year period.

Net loss for the third quarter of 2026 was $5.8 million, or $0.24 per share, compared to a net loss of $7.5 million, or $0.37 per share in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months of 2026, net loss was $21.3 million, or $0.94 per share, compared to $25.7 million, or $1.72 per share in the same period of 2025. Turning to the balance sheet. As of September 30, 2026, PolyPid had cash equivalents, and short-term deposits of $15.5 million, compared to $12.9 million at December 31, 2025.

Our cash at September 30 does not yet include the $15 million milestone payment from Azurity for the NDA acceptance, which is recorded as a receivable on the balance sheet and was received in early October. Our plans for PD01B over the next 18 months involve relatively modest spending and are reflected in this outlook. Based on our current plans and assumptions, we believe that our existing cash resources, together with the expected proceeds from our commercialization agreement with Azurity, as well as future potential proceeds, will be sufficient to fund operations into 2028 and through several significant upcoming potential milestones. With that, we will now open the call for questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Chase Knickerbocker from Craig-Hallum.

Chase Knickerbocker: Good morning. Thanks for taking the questions, and congrats on the progress. On the label, I respect that you are not going to talk about specifics, but can you just confirm for us that labeling discussions themselves have occurred with FDA? Thanks.

Dikla Akselbrad: Hi, Chase. Good morning. Yes, and we said that in the press release, that we are at the stage of the label discussion with everything that is coming with it.

Chase Knickerbocker: Got it. Thanks. Then just second, as we think about physician feedback from what we have disclosed on PD01B, anything else you have kind of gotten from the clinician community, whether it is your outreach or their outreach, as far as what kind of the product profile that they would look for here? I think particularly just around as we think about this product potentially fitting into kind of current standard of care and how these patients are treated, particularly around kind of bandage changes, et cetera. Thanks.

Dikla Akselbrad: Feel free to add to that also based on the latest conference. Couple of things that we are hearing from colorectal surgeons in particular, and those are very detailed into the data that we show in our phase III. What they really get from this data is obviously the 60% reduction of infection. That is obvious. That is the key secondary, and this is easy for them to know that they have a certain percentage of surgical site infection in these patients. It is shown to be reduced by 60%. The other thing that they do, they look at, they also look at the. Those are, of course, open procedure.

The other thing that they mentioned to us, and this was coming almost from everyone that we spoke with, is the fact that the bottom line of our incident of surgical site infection with D-PLEX was lower than what they see in their minimally invasive business. This is really encouraging. The other thing that is a focal point for all of the discussion is the understanding that when you look at the infection that are still there after the reduction that we have done, and you compare the complexity of those patients and those infection between the two arms, you see the same level of reduction in complexity.

That imply that patients are not just having fewer event, but also that they have the same level of complexity, maybe even less complexity in the fewer infection that are there. These are two major, I think, focal points. Ori, anything you want to add to it?

Ori Warshavsky: Sorry, I was on mute. I was on mute. I would just add that surgeons, before they go into these procedures, they assess the patient based on risk. Again, what D-PLEX does is help reduce some of this risk and mitigate this risk. This is kind of how they triage the patient, and this is how they prepare. I think this is what they will gain most from, or when they think of where to apply or where to use the product, it is really based on the risk assessment.

We know from literature, we know from data that risk factors, smokers, diabetics, high BMI, older patients have higher risk for infection, and this will be kind of the target for the product.

Chase Knickerbocker: Got it. Maybe just last from me. Any kind of conversations as part of this review that kind of give you a sense for how FDA is thinking about kind of the bar for you on label expansion, particularly into broader abdominal surgeries? Thanks.

Dikla Akselbrad: We discussed this briefly on our R&D Day about two weeks ago, but also in our prepared remark today. This is ongoing. So the expansion from colorectal to abdominal, this is a work that is internally on the motion, and we said that we plan to initiate those discussion with the FDA this quarter. So you can imagine that the package to the FDA is up and ready. We will be submitting it this quarter. I think it's premature to discuss what the requirements will be before we actually hear from the FDA. But we think we have a very good case to expanding from colorectal, and specifically from these broad phase III data to abdominal.

But let's wait until we hear from the agency.

Operator: Your next question comes from Jason Butler from Citizens.

Jason Butler: Hi. Thanks for taking the questions, and congrats on the progress. Two questions. Maybe a quick follow-up to the label expansion question. Given the funding commitment from Azurity, how quickly do you think you can start to look at surgeries beyond abdominal surgery? Is that something that could even happen in parallel, or do you expect it to be a sequential process? Then second question, Dikla, can you maybe just comment a little bit more about your expectations for the ramp in adoption throughout 2027, and to what extent is the or how important will the NTAP be to driving adoption? Thank you.

Dikla Akselbrad: Sure. Good morning, Jason. So, we are prepared and ready, and label expansion is very important both for Azurity and to us. This is one of our major levers of growth. We've discussed this very detailed, looking at PolyPid into 2030. We view this as the most, or maybe I shouldn't say the most, but one of the most rewarding expansion that we could pursue around D-PLEX100. This is the same way that Azurity looks at it, and it was important for them to have the ability to expand to other surgery. This is why it is covered with our mutual agreement.

To tell you whether things could be running in parallel or one after the other, it won't be smart to go into that when we have an FDA discussion, or we are initiating a discussion very soon. I think this is something we'll need to comment once we hear the feedback. But presumably, there are specific surgeries or specific area that could be done in parallel. I'm not sure if this is the best way to do things in parallel.

It could be in a specific area within the area of abdominal and soft tissue, but maybe there are area where we first need to see or to build a strategy with the FDA to convince them that after having additional safety data, additional proof, this could be done. We'll also need to see how this is adopted in the market to the sense that we'll hear from surgeons, we'll hear from hospital, where they want to see this next. So I think this is also something that is important. Ori, you want to touch the second question about the NTAP?

Ori Warshavsky: Yeah, I'll take it. Jason, good morning. You had two questions on ramp-up and NTAP. First on the ramp-up, the plan is really once the product is approved early 2027 to start with launch activities. Launch activities mean that the MSLs are out there to the target hospitals, finding those champions, the surgeons that can bring the product to P&T. Then P&T needs to review, get additional input from their economic assessment, from the quality pay folks, from the infectious diseases specialists. Then after this review, an update to the electronic systems to be added to formulary. It's a process that takes a little bit of time, and it's a process that is done really account by account.

Some hospitals are reviewed, the P&Ts convened every month, and some every quarter. Some of the IDNs review hospital by hospital, and some do one review for the entire network. We will see over the next several months, accounts coming in a sense, in a stepwise approach. One quarter there'll be a set, and then the next quarter will be either more or less, depending on the cadence within the hospital. Without really giving a I know I'm not giving you a specific date, but it will a process that will take several months until we start really seeing traction. It connects also to the NTAP.

When we ask in market research, we ask pharmacists that lead P&T committees about the willingness to put the product on formulary and in stock, there was very high, close to 90% willingness to put the product on formulary. Then we asked them, "Okay, how would the NTAP change your answer?" The answer was, "Okay, from 90% this would go to 100%." They would want to see the data holds without NTAP, meaning the pharmacoeconomic data holds without NTAP, and then NTAP comes in as an addition just kind of to make the decision easier to accept. Timing-wise, it'll be, so if the NTAP application was submitted, it will be approved in August, so and in effect next October.

Really, as P&Ts complete their assessment and ready to put the product on the formulary and for surgeon to use it, NTAP will be there active and ready to go.

Operator: Your next question comes from Boobalan Pachaiyappan from Roth Capital.

Boobalan Pachaiyappan: Good morning, team. Thanks for taking our questions. So obviously the PDUFA date is just three weeks away. Can you explicitly confirm whether the preapproval manufacturing site inspections have been completed, and is there any unresolved observation, for example, Form 483, something like that? Are there any compliance issues? Are there any other deficiencies that were unearthed during this time? If you can confirm that. Thank you. That's the first.

Dikla Akselbrad: Hi. Good morning. Thank you for that. I would say like that. Obviously, as a matter of practice, the FDA is part of the NDA review. It is a standard process that the FDA conduct a preapproval inspection of our manufacturing facility. But I think that at the stage that we are, as a matter of practice, we should not comment on any specific labeling and timing status of preapproval inspection. We said in the press release that everything has been either set to support the regulatory milestone or has already been done. PDUFA is in just about two weeks. I think we have to be patient.

We are standing behind everything that we said, both in terms of the timing and the label discussions that are underway. That by itself is a strong signal to where the review process is. We'll need to be patient a little bit more.

Boobalan Pachaiyappan: That is super helpful. Thanks for that. In terms of Azurity, trying to do all the pre-launch activities. I am just curious whether they are finding out hospitals where there is very low baseline infection rates or operatives with more intensive prevention protocols, because in those cases, the economic case for D-PLEX use could be a little bit more challenging. I am just curious if you can comment, maybe you just mentioned the hospital economic evidence.

Dikla Akselbrad: Sure. I will start, and Ori, please add on. They are looking first on First, you need to remember that Azurity has a pipeline of products around mechanical bowel prep. They are speaking with the colorectal surgeon now on a daily basis, and they have their KOLs and the surgeon that they are frequently in contact with. They also have our KOL that has been with us along the development and during the clinical studies. They are the first candidate for approaching. Those are the ones that they are looking at to reach out to first. Ori, you want to add to that something?

Ori Warshavsky: Yes, I think, that is the first step. The second step is, and this is really in line with how we saw the market, is really to go to the academic centers where guidance are written. What I heard when I spoke to some of the surgeons in the academic centers is really, it is almost kind of a race to who has the best technology. If you do not adopt a new technology and your peer across the street does, and they now show better results, or they have something that is more interesting that patients coming in, they kind of compete on the same patient.

Although in some of these academic centers, the infection rates are maybe lower than in some of, let us say, general hospitals or community hospitals, they do have interest to bringing the newest technology, the most effective one, and they are competing between themselves on what to use and how they are measured compared to other top hospitals. That is the kind of the next level of target hospitals that Azurity is looking at.

Operator: Your next question comes from [indiscernible] Larsen from Oppenheimer.

Unknown Analyst: This is Jeevan on for Les. Thanks for taking our questions. First one is, when should we expect pricing disclosure? What net cost per procedure are you discussing with the hospitals, and maybe how that compares with the expected savings from preventing infections? Then, follow-up is, does FDA approval alone trigger the Azurity milestone, or are there other label conditions attached to that? When would the cash be received, and when would that revenue be recognized?

Dikla Akselbrad: Welcome. In terms of the pricing, Azurity will share the pricing at the launch. This is obviously their decision. I can say that up until now, everything that they've learned is very much in line with what we have seen. We obviously shared with them our past market research. Some of the highlights of those were disclosed by us in the past, but this will be their part to disclose. Ori, you want to add anything to that?

Ori Warshavsky: No, that's how it is. The pricing will be decided ultimately by Azurity.

Dikla Akselbrad: As for the second part around milestone, around approval, so as everyone probably recall, we received already $30 million, and there are over $290 million in development, regulatory, and sales milestone. We did not disclose the breakdown of these over $290 million between the three. What we did say is that the development and regulatory milestone are all relatively in the short term. Other than that, I can't really add much to that.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your question comes from Brandon Folkes from H.C. Wainwright.

Brandon Folkes: Maybe just one multi-part from me. How much health economic benefit data do you envision hospitals to require for uptake initially? I know you had generated some good health economic data in the past. So does that still hold for launch, or do you anticipate having to generate new or updated data for the hospitals? Along those lines, do you expect some of the hospitals to run their own experience trials before broad adoption? How large of an investment into post-approval real-world data are you and Azurity contemplating? Thank you.

Dikla Akselbrad: Ori, you want to take this one?

Ori Warshavsky: Yes, I'll take it. Hey, Brandon. The data that we have, we believe is sufficient for launch. This is from our conversations. We've shown, just as Dikla mentioned earlier, we've shown a reduction in the severity of infection, a reduction or a delay in the onset of breakthrough infection, which is very important to the hospitals, because if the patient is discharged, then the whole economics change. We've shown a reduction in length of stay overall for the hospital. So, we believe we have sufficient data for what is needed to demonstrate the economic case in front of P&T. Now, we also had conversations with a number of hospitals regarding your question on, let's call it, the pilot study.

The overall consensus is that if there will be a need for a pilot study, it will be a small handful of patients, seven to 10 patients, something on this level, really to check how the surgeons are comfortable with the product. It wouldn't be an efficacy study, but more really to understand the usability and how it works with the workflow of the operating room. So, that is something that is expected, that is something that Azurity is looking for. Beyond that, the post-approval kind of real-world data, I think it's a little bit early to discuss. In any case, it will be part of the tactics of Azurity on how they drive demand in the market.

But of course, we will support them with our data as needed.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's question and answer session. I will now hand back for closing remarks.

Dikla Akselbrad: Thank you all for joining us today and for your questions. With our PDUFA goal date fast approaching, Azurity preparing for launch, our MAA under review in Europe, and advancing PD01 development, we look forward to updating you on our progress in the weeks and months ahead. As always, we are grateful to our team, our partners, and our shareholders for their continued support. Operator, you may now close the call.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3165. Samsung’s new SmartTag 3 debuts with next-gen Bluetooth – and one big problem

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The Galaxy SmartTag 3 supports emerging Bluetooth tracking tech, but it's not a match for Samsung's OS exclusivity.

Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag 3 is now available for purchase in the US, promising a smaller, lighter design than previous generations, compatibility with iOS devices, 550 days of battery life, an NFC-powered Lost Mode, Left Behind Alerts, and an IP67 dust- and water-resistant rating.

Though the Galaxy SmartTag 3 is compatible with iOS devices, the features available to Apple fans are limited, with Ring Phone, Left Behind Alerts, and Compass View reserved for Galaxy users. Compass View is enabled by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, an upgraded Bluetooth distance-finding technology. Despite Samsung embracing a low-cost boost to device tracking, Channel Sounding is locked inside the Galaxy ecosystem, a blow to the technology’s intended purpose.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Channel Sounding is also Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, but these manufacturers open the technology to all compatible Android phones. However, Samsung’s SmartTag 3 doesn’t rely on Android’s vast but fragmented Find My Device network; instead, Samsung’s take on Channel Sounding will rely exclusively on the Galaxy Find Network. If a semi-closed ecosystem can help make evolving Bluetooth tech more reliable, does it matter that its implementation is counterproductive?

Samsung is the Goldilocks of device ecosystems. It’s not considered a walled garden like Apple, but it’s not as open to full third-party interoperability as Google. Many of Samsung’s most useful features are reserved for use within its Galaxy ecosystem. However, Samsung’s OS is built on top of Android, allowing for more flexibility than iOS, but still offering OS-exclusive features and, more importantly, feature reliability.

Full access to Samsung’s Galaxy Find Network is exclusive to Galaxy devices, similar to how full access to Apple’s Find My tracking features is reserved for Apple devices. On the other hand, Google’s Find Hub can accommodate Android phones from several manufacturers, including Samsung.

Also: Android is getting my favorite iOS tracking feature – what to expect

According to a press release, nearly 900 million Galaxy devices exist on the Galaxy Find Network. Each one’s constant Bluetooth signals contribute to an expansive network of crowdsourced data, extending the Galaxy FindTag 3’s reach and surfacing location data faster.

Google’s Find Hub’s greatest benefit is its scale: it can work with headphones, earbuds, Bluetooth trackers, smartphones, and smartwatches from multiple manufacturers.

However, different ecosystems limit tracking features to basic functionality, showing only where a device was last seen before it was powered off, or emitting a chime if you lose it. Live location data and accurate direction and distance finding from your smartphone aren’t possible.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Implementing Bluetooth Channel Sounding aims to break down ecosystem-specific barriers, especially in a device-tracking context. If your smartphone, headphones, and smartwatch all support Channel Sounding, you could access fine-ranging tracking on all of them, regardless of device manufacturer.

Despite Samsung’s ecosystem providing it a device-tracking advantage, it defeats the purpose of Bluetooth: democratization. Basic Bluetooth connectivity allows any Bluetooth-compatible device to connect to another; that’s why you can wirelessly pair a pair of AirPods with a Lenovo laptop.

Also: Google’s Pixel Tag tracker has a big advantage over AirTags

Channel Sounding’s goal is no different in that it aims to bring more accurate distance awareness to Bluetooth-enabled devices, allowing you to finely track a pair of Sony headphones with an iPhone — that’s the goal, but not yet reality.

Samsung instead adopted Channel Sounding for its first consumer-ready endpoint within the boundaries of its ecosystem. Only Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy S26 Ultra, and Galaxy S26 Plus users can unlock the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding capabilities when engaging its Compass View feature.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

All of these phones support Bluetooth 6.0 and Channel Sounding, but the Galaxy SmartTag 3’s Channel Sounding abilities will only be available to them and future Galaxy phones with Channel Sounding.

Conversely, Google’s Pixel Tag offers Channel Sounding to all Android phones that support it, including Galaxy phones. The result is that the Galaxy SmartTag 3 will operate just like any other Bluetooth tracker when paired with a base-model flagship phone, an older Galaxy phone, or an iPhone.

During this year’s WWDC, Apple announced Channel Sounding support for iPhones with its N1 networking chip and third-party Bluetooth 6.3 devices. Bluetooth 6.3 devices aren’t on the market yet and won’t be for a few years.

I assume Apple’s announcement of faraway future support is to give itself time to decide how Channel Sounding will fit into its walled garden, similar to Samsung’s implementation in the Galaxy SmartTag 3.

Also: How to tell if a hidden AirTag is tracking you – and disable it ASAP

Sure, Google’s Find Hub still needs some maturing; just last year, Google boosted the opt-in opportunities to add more devices for crowdsourced data, Find People is coming to Wear OS, and Find Hub is getting “Notify when left behind” alerts soon.

Apple’s and Samsung’s device location networks may be more feature-rich thanks to their closed ecosystems, but Google is working toward a truly open, easy-to-use network of devices powered by Channel Sounding. Which one is more important to you is for you to decide when it’s time to make a purchase.

#3164. Your November Stargazing Calendar: Meteors, Morning Planets and a Supermoon

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Darker evenings after the end of daylight saving time, plus a crowded morning sky, give you plenty of chances to look up this month.

Looking to see some amazing sights in the autumn sky? You’re in luck. November is the final full month of fall, and with daylight saving time having ended on Nov. 1, the sun has been setting even earlier. That’s good news, since some of November’s best views come before sunrise.

Venus, Mercury, Mars and Jupiter all appear in the morning sky this month, with Mars and Jupiter drawing close together around Nov. 15–16. The Leonid meteor shower peaks a couple of nights later, and the hours after moonset on Nov. 17–18 offer the darkest window to catch it. Evenings have their own highlights, from Saturn after dusk to the Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24.

Below, find some of the remaining sights you should catch in the night sky throughout the rest of November.

Every planet is visible during the month of November, though depending on the time and day, you’ll get a better or worse view of them. Mercury and Venus are the most difficult to see due to their proximity to the sun.

Mercury: Mercury was at its eastern elongation during October, so it starts November a bit too close to the sun to see safely. It reaches western elongation on Nov. 20, when it’ll be easily visible just before sunrise for the rest of the month.

Venus: Venus starts the month just ahead of the sun at sunrise, technically making it possible to see every morning in November. It gets further from the sun as the month goes on, making it easier and safer to see toward the end of the month.

Mars: Mars is high in the sky all month. It rises out of the eastern horizon shortly after midnight at the start of November and rises earlier as the month progresses. Early morning is the best time to see it, or right around midnight toward the end of the month.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are close pals for all of November, rising at roughly the same time and right next to each other in the sky. The star Regulus joins in to form a trio, which is visible to the naked eye the entire month.

Saturn: Saturn is also visible every night in November. It’s in the eastern sky when the sun sets, and sets on the western horizon shortly before sunrise. Right after dark is the best time to see it, but you’ll need binoculars or a telescope to capture its glorious rings.

Neptune: Neptune and Saturn are teamed up for November, with both of them being very close in the sky and following a similar trajectory. Bring binoculars or a telescope.

Uranus: Uranus is in the night sky every day in November, rising in the east shortly before sunset and setting in the west right around sunrise. It reaches opposition on Nov. 25, which means it’s as far away from the sun as it can get, and will be the most visible. You’ll still want to bring some binoculars or a telescope for best results.

Most of the planets are visible in the night sky almost every night in November, but on Saturday, there’ll be a fun little planet parade. It’ll take place just before sunrise, so it’s mostly for early risers. Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter are set to line up nicely, making them easy to spot. This is especially true for Jupiter and Mars, which should be right next to each other that night.

The show will start around Saturday and will last until around Nov. 25, depending on your location. The tricky part is catching Mercury in the sky before the sun comes up. It’s only about a 30-minute window since the sun closely follows Mercury up over the eastern horizon. The single best day to view it is Nov. 20, when Mercury is at its western elongation — as far from the sun as it can get.

Uranus is also visible at this time, bringing the number of visible planets to three. Saturn and Neptune are below the horizon. Uranus is on the other side of the sky, however, so it’s not technically part of the alignment.

If you miss the Southern Taurids, you only have to wait a week to catch a glimpse of the Northern Taurids meteor shower. This is another long-lasting meteor shower that started on Oct. 20 and runs until Dec. 10. It peaks on Wednesday and Thursday morning. The American Meteor Society notes that the moon is only 5% illuminated on Wednesday, giving viewers even better conditions than during the Southern Taurids.

It is otherwise virtually identical to the Southern Taurids. The shower appears to originate from the same constellation, Taurus, which rises and sets at almost exactly the same times as it did a week earlier. The Northern Taurids promise about five meteors per hour under optimal conditions, with an increased chance of fireballs. Both showers are even fueled by the same comet, 2P/Encke. It’s the space equivalent of a sitcom rerun airing just one week later.

Leonids is usually the most active meteor shower in November. It started on Nov. 6 and runs until Nov. 30, making it shorter than both Taurids meteor showers. It peaks on the evening of Nov. 16 and the morning of Nov. 17.

The good news is that the meteor shower is very easy to find. Meteors from it will appear to originate from the Leo constellation, which is right next to Mars and Jupiter, which are visible in the night sky.

The bad news is that this part of the sky doesn’t rise until around midnight, making this a meteor shower for night owls. It should produce about 15 meteors per hour under optimal conditions, though you can expect slightly fewer because the 41% illuminated moon will create enough natural light pollution to obscure fainter meteors.

The Leonids have produced exceptional meteor storms in the past, with hundreds of meteors per hour. That isn’t expected to happen in 2026, but the odds aren’t zero. They may improve after the comet loops around the sun again in 2031.

A micro moon is noticeably smaller and less bright than a supermoon or even a regular full moon.

November’s Beaver Moon takes place just two days before Thanksgiving. It is also the first of a string of four consecutive supermoons that will close out 2026 and begin 2027. This happens when the moon is within 90% of perigee — its closest point to Earth. The phenomenon makes the moon appear about 7% larger than a regular moon and 14% larger than a minimoon — and noticeably brighter than both.

Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, the Beaver Moon reaches its peak illumination on Nov. 24 at 9:53 a.m. ET, which is after sunrise for most people in the US. That means the best time to see it is either the night before (Nov. 23) or the evening after (Nov. 24). The moon remains over 90% full from Nov. 22-27. If you plan on going skygazing, avoid those days like the plague, since the moon creates a ton of light pollution.

It’s not often that the same event happens twice in a single month, but it turns out Jupiter, Mars and the moon just can’t seem to get enough of each other. The trio closes out the month the same way it started: hanging out very close together in the night sky. And yes, Regulus will once again tag along.

Unlike the prior meetup, this one only lasts for one night before the moon dashes away. Since all four of them are visible with the naked eye and the moon is still mostly full, people shouldn’t have any trouble finding them. Eagle-eyed stargazers may see Algieba nearby as well. It’s the second brightest star in the Leo constellation (behind Regulus), and it’s also visible without binoculars or a telescope.

The constellations continue their summer-to-winter shakeup. Prominent constellations in the sky include Taurus, Pegasus, Capricornus, Aquila, Pisces and Aries. Mainstays such as the Big Dipper and Little Dipper are still out there, but can be difficult to see if you live too far south. As a rule, we recommend using a sky map or a tool such as Stellarium to pinpoint each object.

There are also some lesser-known asterisms to seek out, such as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters), the Great Square of Pegasus and the Circlet of Pisces. The Summer Triangle is still visible, while the Winter Triangle becomes much easier to spot as it rises above the horizon earlier in the evening.

#3162. Android Auto requires Android 11 or higher now – check your compatibility

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Android Auto's minimum requirements have changed. Here's what to know.

Google has officially phased out support for Android 9 and Android 10 for wired Android Auto use — so you’ll need Android 11 at a minimum to connect an Android phone to a compatible car via USB, according to an update to Google’s Android Auto support page spotted by Android Authority. Android 11 through Android 17, the most up-to-date version, are fully supported for Android Auto (though Android 17’s adoption rate remains quite low).

These changes confirm early reports that Android 10 users saw warnings that their devices would soon lose Android Auto support, even before Google’s documentation had specified the change.

Also: Got an old car? Android Auto is easy to add: 2 ways, starting at $20

It’s not uncommon for Google to drop the oldest Android versions that can still run Android Auto every few years. In 2024, Android 8, released in 2017, was dumped from service. Android 11 was first released in 2020.

Android Auto brings apps to your car display so that drivers can focus better on the road. It allows you to control features such as navigation, maps, calls, text messages, and music, and is the Android equivalent of Apple CarPlay.

Also: 5 Android Auto apps that make my life easier on the road

The requirements have changed little since last year, aside from the new minimum software requirement. The new instructions for wired Android Auto support are straightforward: Phones must be running Android 11 (Red Velvet Cake) or newer, have an active data plan, and be supported by a compatible car. Google also recommends a quality USB cable.

Android Auto is integrated into compatible phones, so you do not need to download it. Android Auto isn’t available on devices that run Android (Go edition).

Also: I was a big wireless Android Auto fan, until I tried wired – now I won’t go back

To find out if your car or stereo is compatible with Android Auto, Google has a hub page to help. For more information about your car’s compatibility with Android Auto on your car display, it’s best to contact your vehicle manufacturer.

For drivers still using older phones running Android 9 or Android 10, getting Android Auto back will require either replacing a current device with one that runs Android 11 or newer, or installing an available software update on a current device.

#3161. Apple TV Adds Sign Language Interpretation, Starting With Original Film ‘Being Heumann’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Streaming Services

It's the latest streaming service to add American and British Sign Language options, making movies more accessible and enjoyable for a wider audience.

Apple TV is adding sign language interpretation for a handful of supported streaming titles, beginning with the Apple original film Being Heumann, which premieres on Friday.

With iOS 27.2, you’ll find new options for American Sign Language and British Sign Language within Apple TV’s app settings. When you select one of these languages, a new button will appear on supported Apple original titles indicating sign language availability. You can also turn off or change your language selection directly within the player.

Titles that support sign language interpretation will have a sign language icon displaying an image of a hand. This icon appears on the title page of a show or movie, next to other accessibility options like closed captions and audio descriptions.

Being Heumann is an apt pick for debuting this accessibility feature. The film centers on the true story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) and her leadership in the historic 1977 protest that helped advance equal rights and protections for Americans with disabilities. Sign language support will also roll out to other Apple TV titles starting with F1 The Movie, followed by Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid (which debuts Nov. 25) later this year.

Apple TV is adding a dedicated collection called Movies & Shows with American Sign Language to make it easier to browse supported content. That collection will include movies where sign language is part of the story, such as 2021’s Oscar-winning film CODA. You can also look up “with ASL” in the app’s search bar to find relevant titles.

“We believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives, said in a statement. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences.”

Apple TV joins a handful of other streaming platforms with sign language options, including HBO Max and Prime Video. Netflix also features sign language interpretation for dozens of kids and family titles through a partnership with SignUp Media, which built a Chrome extension that overlays an interpreter onto supported shows and movies. SignUp is also available on select Disney Plus and Peacock content.

While closed captioning can help some deaf and hard-of-hearing people better understand what’s happening on screen, many viewers prefer watching with sign language interpretation, which can better convey emotion and expression.

“For the deaf community, our first language is ASL,” Nakia Smith, a deaf storyteller and an interpreter for the HBO Max series It: Welcome to Derry, told me in an interview earlier this year.

Unlike closed captioning, which has become nearly ubiquitous across streaming and television, sign languages like ASL are slowly making their way into more entertainment spaces, from sports broadcasts to awards ceremonies and red carpets. But there’s still a long way to go.

The challenge is that sign language interpretation requires skilled human professionals who can capture context and nuances, which takes time and resources. More companies appear to be making the effort. And while some studios are exploring AI to automate captioning, the complexity and diversity of sign languages suggest this will remain a largely human-driven endeavor for the foreseeable future.

For its part, Apple worked closely with the deaf community, partnering with Directors of Artistic Sign Language to ensure they matched the tone of the films and maintained authentic representation.

“It’s incredibly meaningful to see our beautiful language authentically represented onscreen,” Daniel Durant, who appears in Being Heumann and who directed the film’s sign language interpretation, said in a statement. “Bringing this experience to life required a lot of care to ensure every translation captured the emotion and meaning of the story. I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences.”

Jennifer Buell: Thank you, Stefanie. Good morning, and thank you for joining us. These cells read the disease and respond to it.

These data were exemplified in the same year at the American Thoracic Society, the Military Health Science and Research Symposium and the Society for Immunotherapy in Cancer, where we added lung, clinical and senolytic data that I will cover shortly. Our strategy is deliberately focused. We're using randomized evidence in severe hypoxemic respiratory failure to establish a rapid development pathway for agenT-797. And with the validation of this technology, the case for deployable immune restoration in critical illness. We extend this platform into fibrosis, cancer and engineered iNKT medicines where the biology is differentiated.

Our capital deployment is focused on our randomized readout, the biomarker work that explains it, the regulatory execution and the reliable supply, and I'll take you through each piece in turn. First, our global named patient access program. In the third quarter of this year, we recognized pre-commercial product revenue, our first, from agenT-797 supplied on a paid per patient basis under our named patient import pathway in collaboration with Orphan Drug Consulting and BAP, now open in multiple countries outside of the United States. agenT-797 is investigational, thus every paid named patient request originates with a treating physician and is authorized on a case-by-case basis by regulators.

This program shows 3 things: One, the product we manufacture and hold in inventory here in Lexington, Massachusetts can support a clinical program and physician-directed access at the same time. We can reliably move a cryopreserved cell products across borders and physicians are requesting it for patients with serious unmet medical needs outside of our clinical trials. This infrastructure is a template we intend to apply in additional markets. In August, our program was a plan, and today, it's active in treating patients. This is the pace at which we intend to execute the rest of our strategy. Turning to acute lung injury and ARDS, our randomized Phase II program.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome, or ARDS, is one of the largest unsolved problems in critical care. We estimate that approximately 93,000 U.S. patients a year fall within our initial target population of ventilated pneumonia-associated moderate to severe ARDS. Based on our current modeling, that represents a substantial annual market opportunity with potential to expand into other causes of severe lung injury. Our randomized placebo-controlled Phase II study of 797 plus standard of care in adults with acute lung injury and moderate to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure continued enrolling in Lviv, Ukraine during this quarter. U.S. activation is in its final stages, and we expect to begin dosing in the U.S. before year-end. In August, Dr.

Hammond presented initial day 28 observations from the first treated patients at the MHSRS conference, the first look we guided to you for the second half of 2026. We observed no major serious adverse events attributed to 797, and we can now extend that picture to additional treated patients. The comparative readout is expected in 2027, reflecting the planned pace of our enrollment. We plan to refine the study as an adaptive Phase IIb/III study, a seamless Phase III study. The initial randomized stage will enroll about 124 patients with the ability to expand to as many as 300 patients. The proposed endpoint is hierarchical, survival without VV-ECMO at day 14, followed by all-cause mortality through day 28.

We plan to meet with the FDA before year-end to discuss the design, including whether the randomized stage can contribute directly to a registration-enabling Phase III. Alignment on this design would make the path to registration materially more efficient. Acute lung injury is fundamentally a failure of immune regulation, uncontrolled infection, dysregulated inflammation and impaired immune repair at once. iNKT cells read the tissue environment and direct the response and agenT-797 appears to deliver from inventory without apheresis, HLA matching or lymphodepletion. To put this into clinical context, I'm going to turn the call over to Dr. Terese Hammond. She leads our inflammatory and pulmonary programs and actively practices critical care medicine. Terese Hammond: Thank you, Jen. I actively treat patients in the ICU as Jen mentioned, and ARDS is one of the conditions I see most often and can do the least about. My first experience with agenT-797 was during the Phase I/II trial during the COVID pandemic, and that is why I joined this effort. Roughly 40% to 50% of these patients die. And after decades of trials, there's still no approved drug shown to reduce that mortality. What we offer today is support, the ventilator proning and when all else fails veno-venous ECMO. We keep patients alive and wait for the immune system to rigth itself, but in a large percentage of cases, that doesn't happen.

What struck me about the first patients treated in Lviv was this pattern. They are very sick patients with multidrug-resistant infections, yet their fevers resolved, their oxygenation rapidly improved. They came off the ventilator and vasopressors and immune markers in both blood and bronchoalveolar lavage lung fluid tracked their recovery. The endpoint survival without ECMO at day 14, then mortality at day 28 maps to the decisions we actually make at the bedside, because agenT-797 comes from inventory with no matching or conditioning, it can be given in the window, the very first few days when it really matters. It can be thawed, it can be given in any ICU, it can be infused simply. There's a second reason this matters to me. Many ARDS survivors leave the ICU with lungs that keep scarring, driven by the same inflammation, senescent cells and activated fibroblasts behind the interstitial lung diseases that I see beyond the ICU in the clinic.

Many of these ILDs have no treatment options beyond transplant or palliative care. If these cells can also clear the senescent cells that sustain fibrosis, modify or modulate chronic inflammation as the preclinical work Jen just described suggests, the same therapy that we're using in studying for acute lung injury could reach well beyond the ICU and into the clinic and into other interstitial lung diseases. With that, I'd like to turn it back to you, Jen.

Jennifer Buell: Thank you so much, Terese. In September, 797 was selected as a therapeutic cell system for the ARPA-H BioStabilization Systems or BoSS program, where ARPA-H is committing up to $87 million over a 4-year period to move living medicines from cryogenic storage toward room temperature. Cold chain is the single largest barrier to taking an allogeneic cell therapy beyond specialized centers. We've already delivered 797 to ventilated patients within days of Ministry of Health authorization in a conflict zone, removing the freezer would let a living immune therapy be stockpiled like a conventional drug in community hospitals and in austere settings. iNKT cells are also a demanding stabilization benchmark, so success here would matter for the whole field.

MiNK participates on a fixed fee basis, which means as we advance and perform, we continue to accumulate and be eligible for reimbursement for our efforts. Finally, our scientific progress. Last week, at the Society of Immunotherapy for Cancer, we presented data in a human organoid model of microsatellite stable colorectal cancer with liver mets, a setting with no approved immune therapy and where BOT and BAL alone produced no significant tumor cell killing. Adding agenT-797 shifted suppressive macrophages towards an antigen-presenting phenotype and unlocked tumor killing. The rationale for the ongoing Phase II study at Scripps led by Dr. Darren Sigal is combining BOT/BAL plus iNKT cells in patients with MSS colorectal cancer with metastatic disease to their liver.

We are excited to present data in the beginning of next year on this program, the clinical program. Also, in collaboration with Dr. Jesús Gil at Imperial College London, we showed that agenT-797 and MiNK-215, our FAP-targeted IL-15-armored CAR-iNKT candidate act as living senolytics. This is very exciting, clearing the senescent zombie cells that chemotherapy and radiation leave behind. MiNK-215 also reaches the FAP-positive stroma that shields tumors and drive scarring. These cells fuel treatment resistance in cancer and progression in fibrotic lung disease, giving us one thread from oncology to the lung and ultimately to aging.

We will continue to develop this data set in sequence, randomized evidence first from our ongoing trial and then into deeper data sets with senescence and fibrosis in the clinic. And finally, our Phase I study in prevention of GvHD is activating at University of Wisconsin. The investigator-sponsored Phase I study of 797 for GvHD prevention funded by the NIAID STTR award and further funded by the Mary Gooze Clinical Trial Award is moving towards first dosing. Our colleagues at UW have informed us that it expects the first patients to be scheduled to dose by December.

The start, while it has moved from our first half guidance, is now moved to the second half, but we certainly expect to activate and enroll patients this year. This study as well as the Scripps Institute study remain nondilutive. These are fully funded externally. I will now turn the call over to Melissa to discuss our financials.

Melissa Orilall: Thank you, Jen. We ended the quarter with $7.5 million in cash and cash equivalents compared to $8.8 million at June 30. Importantly, this quarter, we recognized our very first pre-commercial product revenue from agenT-797 supplied through our named patient program. This program just launched this quarter, and we expect demand to vary from quarter-to-quarter based on physician requests and case-by-case regulatory authorizations. Our net loss for the quarter was $2.6 million or $0.50 per share compared with $2.9 million or $0.65 per share a year ago. The cash used in operation was approximately $1.3 million in the quarter, down from approximately $2.1 million in the second quarter, our lowest quarter of the year.

We are focusing our spend on the randomized study and reducing costs elsewhere. Our G&A expenses decreased 44% to $1 million, primarily from lower professional fees and stock compensation expense. Our R&D expenses increased to $1.8 million from $1.1 million, primarily reflecting the timing of our clinical trial activities, including our randomized Phase II study and preliminary translational analysis presented at major conferences in this quarter. As disclosed in our 10-Q, we will strengthen our balance sheet with additional funding and currently meet the requirements as a going concern. As we announced earlier this quarter, MiNK was selected as a cell therapy provider for the ARPA-H BoSS program, as Jen mentioned.

And we continue to strengthen our balance sheet through partnerships and licensing, nondilutive funding and equity or debt financing with the priority of funding the randomized study through its readout. I will now turn the call back to Jen for closing remarks.

Jennifer Buell: Thank you, Melissa. Now stepping back and looking over the last 5 quarters, we took biology from refractory cancer into critical illness, started a randomized Phase IIb trial, began treating patients through paid access, earned federal validation for deployability and connected our oncology work to our fibrotic lung disease platform. And over the same period, our net loss per share and G&A costs have come down. And we've added a fourth source of nondilutive funding support alongside the STTR award, and that includes the clinical Mary Gooze award as well as our C-Further partnership in advancing our PRAME TCR in pediatric patients with blood cancers.

We are spending where the randomized trial requires it, and our externally funded programs are advancing alongside and not at expense. Our priorities into 2027 are specific: activate the U.S. ICU sites and sustain enrollment in the 1300-02 study, seek FDA alignment on the adaptive Phase IIb/III design and pursue supportive designations that will help to accelerate development. Report comparative data in 2027, support first dosing in our GvHD program, extend our named patient access program into additional markets where regulations allow and of course, advance our collaboration with ARPA-H and deployable cell therapy work. Across cancer and critical illness, the underlying problems we are addressing is a loss of coordinated immune function.

If the early clinical and biologic patterns we are observing hold up under randomized evidence an off-the-shelf therapy that restores that coordination and that can be stocked and delivered like a conventional drug would change what cell therapy can do and where it can be given. The clinical value proposition is intact, and our job really is to advance and protect the readouts that can really validate the platform that we're moving forward. I appreciate your continued support. Thank you for joining us today. Operator, we will now turn the call over for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Mayank Mamtani with B. Riley Securities.

Mayank Mamtani: I appreciate the level of detail remarkable progress on so many fronts. So on the Phase IIb ARDS randomized trial, are you able to share the treatment effect you're assuming on both the absolute mortality rate and then maybe also on the VV-ECMO utilization rates, recognizing there could be differences in care across different geographies. I don't know how you're accounting for that. And then there was a recent Phase III program related regional licensing deal I don't know if you want to maybe put your program in context of how maybe the peer landscape for this disease state is kind of evolving?

And maybe I don't know if you have any thoughts on that Japan-specific license for that antibody that was done recently. And then I have a couple of follow-ups.

Jennifer Buell: Mayank, thank you so much for the questions. I also have Dr. Terese Hammond here to speak a bit about standard of care. So with respect to the data observations to date, we do plan to present and have been invited to do so at some major conferences next year, first half of next year. So we will be releasing more formal data analyses at that time. However, currently, what we are -- what we can tell you is that the observations that we continue to see are validating our observations from the already published Phase I/II study.

So our 28-day mortality is still very consistent with what our observations were earlier, which give us quite a bit of optimism and enthusiasm for the program. And we'll continue to keep you apprised as the data evolve. We plan to be dosing in the United States before the end of this year. Our trial is continuing to enroll in Lviv Ukraine and will then certainly be active, as I mentioned, in the U.S. as well. What I will say is that our program has been designed and protocoled to really standardize for U.S.-like treatment, which means hospital ventilator settings as well as standard of care therapies, available therapies for patients.

So that's an important part of the program so that all patients contributing to the enrollment will be treated in accordance with U.S. treatment guidelines for standard of care. Despite what's available to patients, though, I just want to remind you, mortality remains in patients not treated with the cells of about 40% and sometimes higher than that. We continue to see patients from our previously published data of over 70% to 75% survival rates in our early observations that we're continuing to validate through our Phase II trial. With that, I'll invite Dr.

Hammond to say a few words about the standard of care and the treatment paradigm that we've essentially ensured meets U.S. like treatment paradigms in Lviv Ukraine as well as then, of course, our approach to invite surgical ICUs as well as medical ICUs to programs that are launching in the United States and dosing patients before the end of this year. Terese?

Terese Hammond: Yes, Jen. And thank you, Mayank, for the question. So we've been rigorous about selecting centers. The selection process is active in 4 U.S. centers. but rigorous about making sure that standard of care is adhered to. We also visited Lviv Ukraine prior to deciding on enrolling that site to really validate in person that the same standards we use in the United States when patients are admitted with ARDS are adhered to in the Lviv ICUs. That means patients are getting lung protective therapy. They're getting early antibiotics. They're getting steroids where appropriate. They're being prone when oxygen ratios reach a threshold that's universally felt to be appropriate.

And more importantly, as we move into the U.S. and as we start to enroll patients by year-end, we are selecting U.S. centers that not only have very high ICU censuses of these ARDS patients, both medical and surgical ICUs, but also ones that can rapidly escalate to ECMO based on very conventional standards really put out by ELSO, the Extracorporeal life support organization. So these groups have already demonstrated oftentimes with platinum or gold ELSO designation that they manage their ECMO patients appropriately.

That way, we can try to ensure uniform decision-making in terms of when to escalate to ECMO, and as Jen said, for the Phase II, hopefully seamless Phase III trial, one of the important considerations will be early modification, early improvement in oxygenation so that we can forego or prevent escalation to ECMO.

Jennifer Buell: Thank you very much, I'm sorry, go ahead. I was going to answer your second question. But please go ahead.

Mayank Mamtani: No, no, please go ahead, Jen, on the partnership, if you want to comment on that.

Jennifer Buell: Yes. And so I assume that you're referring to the Edesa agreement, and that's an encouraging example of strategic interest in ARDS overall. We have, as you know, our pursuit to continue to strengthen the balance sheet is really based on nondilutive funding as well as strategic collaborations, which are all very actively advancing. With respect to ARDS, there is a growing interest in this space, and there are, I believe, a couple of reasons for that. The first is that the FDA has now been far more specific about the intended target population definitions around that population and the urgency to bring new therapies forward. Currently, there are no effective approved therapies for patients with ARDS.

The Edesa product is essentially a TLR4 agonist and has demonstrated some activity in earlier phase trials. What we see with our product, though, is not only can we address some of the immune inflammatory components of ARDS. So we very rapidly see that upon administration, we see an anti-inflammatory signature, which is incredibly important in this ICU setting, particularly in patients undergoing critical care with critical illnesses. That anti-inflammatory signal enables essentially the lungs to start healing.

And in addition to the anti-inflammatory, we see pathogen clearance, including in patients in Ukraine who have more than -- 100% of them have one or more multidrug-resistant pathogens, and we have been able to make a meaningful difference for those patients and in particular, clearing some of those pathogens, gram-negative pathogens as well, both important to enable lung healing. And in addition to those multifactors, we also see cytokines that are related to epithelial tissue repair. So in addition to the factors that we're helping to ameliorate to enable lung healing, we also see that the cells are directly impacting molecule -- essentially modulators of lung healing of specific tissue health healing.

We've presented a lot of that publicly, and we're quite excited about what this presents. So with that, I think I appreciate your thinking, and I think that there are a number of reasons as to why you're seeing a growing strategic interest in this space. There are now therapies that actually can make a meaningful impact for patients and the market is recognizing that as well.

Terese Hammond: I was just going to emphasize one point that you made. So here we are sort of 5, almost 6 years post COVID.
