And now 5 years post-COVID also have very high rates of persistent pulmonary disability. So continued fibrosis, continued decrease in lung function, continued issues with return to work and with quality of life.

So I think that, that's also the sort of the aftermath of COVID also has pointed us to the concept that we need to mitigate acute inflammation early completely avoid the progression to chronic inflammation and do something in addition to sort of modulating inflammation to improve recoveries. And I think some of the restorative functions that we've seen in patients treated with cells are very compelling, very provocative.

Mayank Mamtani: Actually, my follow-up was going to be 2-parter on exactly the things you just talked about. On that hyperinflammatory learning you're having about the cells, are there any clear biomarkers that cut across a severe disease state like ARDS or there could be other larger chronic inflammation conditions also that could be relevant? And then my specific question was on the FDA meeting before year-end. If you could maybe just talk about what the different discussion topics that are on the table in context of maybe the specific endpoint, the ECMO free days versus mortality and then maybe also how the Phase II patients count towards the registration cohort and maybe any designation you're pursuing?

Sorry, that was a multiparter, thanks for taking question.

Jennifer Buell: Mayank, thank you so much. I appreciate your rigor. With respect to the biomarkers, we have not yet published the biomarker data set that we've been continuing to accumulate and develop. And there have been -- there's published literature on a developing set of biomarkers that may help not only to identify patients and differentiate them between their inflammatory state hyper and hypo but there also may be similar sets of biomarkers that can help predict response to therapy and identify patients who are more likely to respond to certain types of therapeutic intervention.

And we've got our own developing data set in which we do have what we believe to be an important predictive set of biomarkers that can help us identify patients more quickly who would be more likely to respond. Currently, we're enrolling all patients into the study. We're stratifying them by their biomarker status, and we're continuing to evaluate and validate those markers prospectively in our study. That will be part of a discussion with the agency to help us understand how to identify patients who may be able to benefit more quickly from different therapeutics. Regarding the FDA interactions, we really are seeking their feedback on a couple of things.

One, is a win ratio evaluation for hierarchical endpoint prevention of VV-ECMO, which is a very invasive procedure and also requires one-on-one dedicated ICU nursing staff and respiratory therapy, really essentially by the bedside with great frequency for these patients, incredibly intensive for the patient and also incredibly difficult and intensive for hospitals. And that is an important endpoint for us to be able to restore patients' breathing quickly, prevent ECMO within the first couple of weeks of treatment and then also restore lung function, increase ventilator-free days and enable the patient to have lung healing quickly is a very important outcome for us.

So we want to ensure that we're aligned with the FDA, and we have seen some precedents with this type of a design that has led to approved therapeutics. And our design is really quite consistent with the established precedents so far. So we'll certainly seek their feedback and gain their alignment and partnership, which we have done since the beginning of the program. And in addition to that, we just -- we want to ensure that the patients from the randomized Phase II can contribute to the Phase III in a seamless way.

Therefore, when we have a data readout, which we are anticipating to be around the third quarter of next year, for the initial randomized Phase II trial that those patients will then contribute to the ongoing expanded randomized Phase III, which we believe will move really quite quickly for enrollment so that all patients participating can contribute in a protocol that we hope can support registration of the program ultimately. So we will have -- we will not proceed with aggressivity without great support and partnership with the agency, and that's something that we're continuing to engage them on. And similarly, the biomarkers may help us to speed development and enhance our pathway in a few different ways.

And to the last part of your question, those same biomarkers, which we've just presented at the Society of Immunotherapy for Cancer essentially demonstrate invariant natural killer T cells as effectively something called living senolytics. What we've seen is that these cells not only can restore immunologic activity and function, but also these cells can eliminate senescent cells. And these same senescent cells actually are pro-inflammatory. So these -- by clearing senescent cells, you're actually reducing some of the inflammation cascade that we observe in patients following acute -- acute critical illness like ARDS.

Therefore, if these cells can not only reconstitute immunity, clear inflammation, essentially serve as an anti-inflammatory capability within the lung tissue, clear some of the problematic pathogens that are actually resulting in the inflammatory cascade in the lungs and promote lung healing it could be an extraordinary opportunity for us to bring a meaningful difference to patients in critical care. And those -- the elimination of senescent cells and the elimination of some of these elements that I just mentioned to you and the biomarkers that we're observing, we believe will also prevent progression to some of the long-term fibrotic conditions that impact patients with acute pulmonary disease. Dr.

Hammond mentioned this during her talking points earlier today in the script, and I'll have her reiterate her perspective, but our goal would be not only to get patients out of the ICU, breathing independently and alive, surviving beyond what's currently available to them, but also to prevent the sequelae from that episode, which would be long-term fibrotic lesions in their lungs, which sometimes could lead to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other chronic conditions. We want to eliminate that. Terese?

Terese Hammond: Yes, Jen. I mean, sort of points to some of the work that we're doing with Anne Sperling at the University of Virginia that we've reported on previously, showing that really, it's a spectrum. So acute inflammation that becomes chronic eventually will propagate fibrosis. And in the end, the very most severe form of interstitial lung disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis can then occur. What's really interesting is as a pulmonologist until very recently, I thought that idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is really the end of the line. You either transplanted the patient or you place the patient on palliative care because it's a progressive disease with just a tremendous amount of disability. Dr.

Sperling in her lab has looked at a variety of explanted lungs, looked at the lymph nodes within those lungs. So these are patients that are pending transplant for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other types of fibrosing lung disease. And what she found was astonishing. She found active immune capabilities within these lymph nodes. So these lymph nodes were still active immune sites they were producing germinal centers. And most importantly, when we joined her in a reanalysis, they were depleted of invariant natural killer T cells.

So I think all along the spectrum of acute inflammation, chronic inflammation, fibrosis and ultimately, terminal fibrosis or even cancer, the reconstitution of the immune response, the modulation of inflammation and especially the resolution of acute inflammation, so it doesn't become chronic is a really key perspective here, a really key element here of recovery and certainly plays an enormous role in long-term quality of life and functioning post injury. So the survivors also have sequelae that can be quite debilitating.

Mayank Mamtani: Yes, that explains some of the survival work you intend to do in the future.

Matthew Keller: So switching gears slightly with some just brief questions. I was wondering where does enrollment stand in the colorectal study? And then maybe can you comment on the type of data that we could expect from a future readout from that program?

He's enrolled past the first couple of safety cohorts and the data are accumulating. We expect to have a readout very early in 2027 and have already established the pathway, we believe, to be able to present at probably one of the earliest GI conferences on the cohort. It is not for me to share an update specifically on the patients enrolled, but suffice it to say, there's a meaningful cohort enough so for us to get an impression of the data observations in patients with liver met MSS colorectal cancer.

And again, just for those who are not aware, this is a combination program. The iNKT cells, agenT-797 is administered in combination with botensilimab and balstilimab in patients with MSS colorectal cancer who have metastatic disease to their liver.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] This concludes the Q&A session. I will now turn the call back over to Dr. Jennifer Buell for closing remarks.

Jennifer Buell: Thank you, operator, and thank you all for your continued support. We're incredibly excited about what's to come in the impending weeks to months. So thank you again for joining.

#3159. Top Wall Street analysts see robust growth potential in these 3 stocks

The latest earnings season has eased concerns about a potential artificial intelligence bubble. Increased spending by hyperscalers and other companies has reinforced confidence in the demand for AI infrastructure and software solutions.

Investors keen on capitalizing on the AI boom can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts, who give key insights into a company's ability to capture AI-driven demand despite macro uncertainties and rising competition.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

AI-powered observability and security platform Datadog (DDOG) is this week's first pick. In early May, the company impressed investors with its market-beating first-quarter results and robust outlook.

Following an investor webinar with Vikram Thaker, the senior director of North American business at global consulting firm Cognizant, Bank of America analyst Koji Ikeda reiterated a buy rating on Datadog stock and raised his price target to $260 from $225. The analyst said that following the webinar, he is more positive on the demand backdrop for "best-of-breed infrastructure software vendors" such as Datadog and JFrog. He believes that these two companies have the ability to surpass Bank of America and the Street's estimates.

Ikeda added that the demand for high-quality observability and security platforms like Datadog will increase as enterprises transition to the cloud and AI, making everything more complex. Consequently, he expects the momentum in Datadog's performance to continue.

The five-star analyst highlighted that Datadog delivered first-quarter results that were way above estimates. Also, the second-quarter revenue growth outlook of more than 30% reinforced Ikeda's confidence in DDOG's potential to generate further acceleration in its growth. He emphasized that new large AI-related deals prove Datadog's mission-critical positioning and robust AI-led tailwinds.

"Execution remains top notch, with improving demand trends supporting further beat-and-raise potential," said Ikeda.

Ikeda ranks No. 867 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.4%. See Datadog Hedge Funds Activity on TipRanks.

Micron Technology (MU) stock is having a solid run this year, thanks to unprecedented demand for memory fueled by the ongoing AI boom and elevated pricing stemming from supply challenges. Despite the impressive rally in MU stock, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri significantly raised his price target to $1,625 from $535, while reaffirming a buy rating.

"We believe the market will start to put a more 'normal' multiple on the stock and MU will continue to re-rate higher as more details emerge about the structural changes AI has driven to the entire memory complex," said Arcuri.

Notably, the five-star analyst again raised his calendar years 2027 to 2029 earnings per share estimates, citing traction in long-term agreements across the memory industry. Arcuri highlighted that these new LTAs are of longer durations, involve fixed-volume commitments, and have a partially fixed pricing structure. They are in contrast to offtake agreements in prior periods, which were simply volume-based.

Furthermore, Arcuri's supply chain checks on LTAs across the industry indicate that up to 30% of double data rate memory volumes could soon be locked in at pricing only slightly below current levels. The analyst explained that such agreements will allow Micron to trade some near-term revenue for strong demand visibility and a more stable earnings trajectory.

Based on these LTAs, Arcuri expects Micron's EPS to remain easily above $100 over 2027-2029 and expects the company to deliver $400 billion in free cash flow over this period. Specifically, the analyst raised his 2027, 2028, and 2029 EPS estimates to $155, $167, and $117, respectively, from $133, $122, and $77.

Remarkably, Arcuri ranks No. 2 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 81% of the time, delivering an average return of 56.6%. See Micron Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Lam Research (LRCX), a provider of wafer fabrication equipment and services to the semiconductor industry, is this week's third stock pick. The AI-led surge in semiconductor manufacturing has boosted demand for Lam Research and triggered a strong rally in its shares.

Top Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh increased his price target for LRCX stock to $380 from $330 and reiterated a buy rating. His higher price target reflects strength in demand amid elevated WFE spending.

Rakesh now expects WFE spending to rise 23% to $153 billion in 2026, with 2027 spending to see a 24% surge to $190 billion. In fact, he sees additional upside to these estimates, based on increased capex by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, or TSMC; Samsung; and Micron. Specifically, the total memory WFE investment is projected to be about $112 billion this year.

"With higher revised 2026E/2027E WFE spend, we now see significant upside to consensus estimates for LRCX, MKSI, and AMAT, with LRCX potentially offering the most compelling estimate upside as the steady outperformer vs. WFE and peers," said Rakesh.

Also, the five-star analyst expects the WFE market to continue to benefit from accelerating NAND node transitions, with Lam Research highlighting $40 billion in node transition spending. The majority of this investment is expected before the end of 2027.

Rakesh ranks highly as well. He is #4 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 74% of the time, delivering an average return of 79.2%. See Lam Research Statistics on TipRanks.

#3158. Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

Apple's public-facing satisfaction with the Siri AI launch obscures internal pressures and tensions.

Apple’s recently appointed CEO, John Ternus, is allegedly pushing the company internally to ramp up its AI strategy — including making Siri an AI agent.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the CEO is publicly pleased with the Siri AI launch, but privately encouraging Craig Federighi, Apple’s SVP of software engineering, to move faster.

“Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri,” Gurman wrote. He added that the tension stems from Federighi’s reputation as an AI skeptic.

The revamped Siri AI is now a much better voice assistant with some helpful features. Gurman noted he thinks Siri AI’s ability to automatically fix your weak passwords is already somewhat agentic behavior, though AI-generated passwords have their own issues.

But Siri AI isn’t yet on par with increasingly autonomous agents from AI-first companies that aim to proactively organize your tasks, use your computer, and write advanced code. Still, those rival agents deliver a patchwork of capabilities: while some, like OpenClaw and Anthropic’s Claude Code, are highly functional, others, like Google’s Gemini Spark, aren’t quite there yet.

Also: I tried replacing Claude Code with a free local AI stack

Regardless, the issue here is time. Despite developing powerful hardware perfectly suited for running local AI models, Apple has remained slower than competitors on the AI software front. Competitors have demonstrated they can make promised agent features a reality, some quicker than others.

On the other hand, the fact that Apple hyped Siri AI for two years only to release an improved voice assistant (rather than a groundbreaking AI product) may mean users are ready for more advanced features.

In addition, AI companies are working on their own hardware. “If they can combine that software with AI-native devices designed from the ground up around assistants that see, remember and act, Apple’s longstanding advantages could begin to matter less,” Gurman wrote.

An agentic Siri would most likely build on what users already like about the new version.

The on-screen awareness feature, for example, is currently limited to what’s visible on your screen in that moment, meaning only the part of a long email that you’ve actively scrolled to. An agentic Siri could ideally scroll all the way through an email on its own and surface the insights you’re looking for.

Also: The iPhone made Apple a giant – but the Mac could help it win the AI era

But in the short term, Ternus’ push will likely just deliver on existing promises. Gurman also pointed out that Siri AI still lacks advanced in-app actions, which Apple initially announced in 2024 and would let third-party apps create plug-ins for and pathways through Siri.

“This functionality would let Siri tap into both in-house and third-party applications with more precision,” Gurman wrote. “This past week, as part of the first beta version of iOS 27.3, Apple finally began talking about the feature again.”

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Plus, if we’re talking about agents specifically, newcomers like OpenAI’s Dot and Anthropic’s Duet aren’t competitive themselves yet: ZDNET’s AI vetter-in-residence David Gewirtz found both to be “a little odd” and not “quite ready for prime time”.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks – and all I got was one helpful notification

For users who appreciate the subtlety of Siri AI, though, anything similar to ChatGPT or Claude on their devices might not land, unless each feature is opt-in.

#3157. Google Pixel Tag Hands-On: The AirTag for Android Fans

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Google’s own tracker adds a few welcome details to the smart tracker field.

When a company comes out with its own version of a product in an established market, there has to be a good reason. Maybe it’s created a design that sets the product apart, or it’s included features that none of the competition has.

If you think I’m talking about Apple and Google, you’d be right – but this isn’t the iPhone Duo muscling into the folding phone fray. This time, the roles are reversed: Google is releasing the Pixel Tag, a small Bluetooth tracker that it hopes will be the Android ecosystem’s answer to Apple’s near-ubiquitous AirTag.

The Pixel Tag is available starting Wednesday for $30 each or $100 in a pack of four. It works with Android phones and uses Google’s Find Hub technology for tracking over distances beyond Bluetooth range. If you use an Android phone and have wanted the capability to track things such as keys, bags, bikes, vehicles and other indispensable items, and you want the tech to come from the company that designed the system, the Pixel Tag is an excellent choice.

It isn’t the first Android-compatible tracker. Motorola introduced its Moto Tag 2 earlier this year, and Tile has been the de facto AirTag alternative for several years. There’s also now a growing ecosystem of other items that tap into Apple’s Find My and Android’s Find Hub networks, ranging from slim credit-card-sized devices like the Rolling Square AirCard Pro and Peak Design’s Beacon Finder Card, to novel approaches like Falcam’s TagBatt, a battery for some Sony and Canon mirrorless cameras that integrates Apple Find My tracking.

Google jumping into this more crowded field tells me the company thinks there’s profit to be made by manufacturing its own hardware and software. It’s also investing in the infrastructure it’s already built out, and not leaving the hardware side to a constellation of other vendors.

Trackers like the Pixel Tag and AirTag can be a surprisingly deflating purchase: You pair them with your phone, put them into something you don’t want to lose track of – then forget about them. They’re usually not tactile the way a phone, watch or laptop is each day. And their value doesn’t kick into action until you think an item has gone missing.

After slinging AirTags into bags and dangling them off keychains, one thing I really appreciate about the Pixel Tag is its thinness. Apple chose a small, round footprint, even keeping the exact design for the second-generation AirTags. Google instead opted for a longer lozenge shape, at 1.8 inches (46.1mm), that is about two-thirds the height of the AirTag at 0.2 inch (5.4mm).

Google sent a Bellroy leather keychain as a sample accessory for review, and paired with the Pixel Tag, the two are a fine size for a pocket or clipped to an inside bag pocket. I thought the longer design would get in the way, but it’s not bad at all.

The Pixel Tag uses a CR2032 coin-sized battery that should last about a year (the same as the AirTag). It also has an IP67 rating, which is durable in 1 meter of water for up to 30 minutes.

Another departure from the AirTag is a physical button, making the Pixel Tag even more tactile. When you’re using Find Hub on your phone to locate it by sound, press once to stop the chirps it makes. Or, if you have the tag in hand (on a keychain, for example) and need to find your phone, press twice to ring the phone – it makes a pleasant sing-songy chime that gets louder and more intense as it continues, so I’m confident it’ll be easy to locate, even among couch cushions.

Speaking of the chimes, credit to the Google sound designers who came up with the Pixel Tag’s tune. It has three levels of loudness you can set, and seems plenty audible enough when you’re spelunking the living room for it. I measured it at 80 decibels, which when compared to the second-generation AirTag volume, is 7 less than the 87 decibels of Apple’s tracker.

One more nice touch compared to the AirTag: the Find Hub app shows the tag’s battery status. If that gets to Low or Very Low, the app sends you notifications every two weeks until the battery is replaced. After Apple showed battery statuses on AirTags in early versions of the Find My app, the company changed the Find My app so it only indicates battery when it’s low and needs to be replaced.

The best feature of either tracker is the ability to locate its exact location – not which building or room it’s in, but to tell if the item fell behind the couch or was accidentally dropped in the driveway. (Yes, I’m making up these examples from personal experience.)

Precision Finding uses a combination of Bluetooth 6.0 (via a feature called Channel Sounding) and the ultra-wideband chips inside the tag and the phone to directionally find the tracker when it’s within Bluetooth range. You hold the phone upright, perpendicular to the ground for the best connection. Then you wander your space, watching the indicator change as you get closer to the tag.

On the Pixel Tag, that indication is a wobbly circle shape that fills in as you get closer; when you’re on top of the tracker, the shape is fully filled. The Find Hub app also uses the camera and UWB chip to include an estimated distance in feet and inches (or meters and centimeters). When you’re close enough, the tracking shape becomes a directional arrow to point you the right way. UWB is compatible with the Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8 Fold and newer Pixel phones.

In my testing, the Find Nearby feature performed fairly well. Find Hub using a Pixel 11 Pro XL connected from within about 25 feet, including on multiple levels of a house when I was above or below it.

Perhaps because I was raised on science-fiction devices like the trackers in Aliens, though, I expected more consistent readings. There were times when both I and the tag remained stationary. The distance estimates would fluctuate by several feet.

Since I’ve had this review unit for only a couple of days, I haven’t yet had a chance to send it off with someone else and see if I can track it remotely using the Find Hub network. When nearby Android devices detect the Pixel Tag’s presence, they should securely and privately relay the tracker’s location to Google’s servers. (Apple’s Find My network operates the same way.) I’ll update this article once I’ve taken the tag on such an adventure.

Tracking all your stuff is invaluable – I learned this first-hand earlier this year when I left a small bag containing my passport in a hotel room, and was able to convince the hotel that the bag was still on the premises. But unfortunately, smart tags are being used to track people without their knowledge.

Google is taking the same approach as Apple to help thwart this type of tracking. If a tag is separated from the phone it’s paired with (or the phone of someone else you’ve chosen to share the tag location with), and the tag is moved, its chime activates.

The idea is that you’ll hear an unfamiliar chirp and investigate. It has an NFC chip that displays its information when you tap it using the NFC built into a phone.

#3155. Drug Makers or Biotech Bets: Which ETF Is the Better Buy, State Street’s XPH or First Trust’s FBT?

One fund holds about 60 drug companies at a lower fee. The other holds 30 biotech names and has a stronger long-term record. Either way, expect some volatility.

State Street SPDR S&P Pharmaceuticals ETF (XPH +1.31%) provides broad, low-cost exposure to the pharmaceutical industry, while First Trust NYSE Arca Biotechnology Index Fund (FBT +1.28%) offers concentrated biotechnology exposure with a history of higher returns.

Investors seeking targeted exposure to the healthcare sector often choose between biotechnology and pharmaceuticals. Both funds track life sciences companies, but they differ in their degree of concentration, sub-sector focus, and expense structures, providing distinct risk-reward profiles for those looking beyond a broad healthcare index fund.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-yr return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

The SPDR fund is more affordable than its counterpart, with an expense ratio of 0.35%. This is 20 basis points lower than the 0.55% fee charged by the First Trust fund.

State Street SPDR S&P Pharmaceuticals ETF allocates 100% of its portfolio to the healthcare sector and currently holds 62 positions. Its largest positions include Veradermics (MANE +5.47%) at 2.86%, Xeris Biopharma Holdings (XERS +4.36%) at 2.76%, and Pacira Biosciences (PCRX -0.08%) at 2.51%. The fund was launched in 2006.

First Trust NYSE Arca Biotechnology Index Fund also focuses exclusively on the healthcare sector but maintains a much more concentrated portfolio of 30 holdings. Top positions include Genmab (GMAB -0.37%) at 4.89%, Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (REGN +4.73%) at 3.95%, and Halozyme Therapeutics (HALO -1.26%) at 3.77%. The fund was launched in 2006.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

Healthcare has been making plenty of headlines lately, from the boom in GLP-1 weight-loss drugs to a busy stretch of biotech acquisitions. For long-term investors heading into 2027, the State Street SPDR S&P Pharmaceuticals ETF (XPH) looks like the better way to play it. It costs less than First Trust's biotech fund, holds roughly 60 companies, and pays a small dividend.

XPH is not a big-pharma fund, though. Its equal-weight approach gives smaller drug developers as much influence as the giants, and it has taken deep drops in the past. That makes for a bumpier ride than the name suggests. Still, owning twice as many companies as FBT means one failed trial hurts less, and the smaller names give it room to run when bigger drugmakers come shopping.

FBT owns about 30 biotech companies in equal amounts, has the stronger long-term record, and pays no dividend. It works best as a smaller add-on for those seeking additional biotech risk. XPH's lower fee and broader lineup make it the better core holding for most long-term investors.

#3154. AMD confirms GPU driver bug is wearing out your SSD – how to stop it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

AMD has admitted a bug within its External Events Utility is wearing out SSDs, and promises a fix.

Under normal circumstances, an SSD might go all day without needing to access or write files. But for some AMD Radeon users, anything but normal circumstances are causing drives to continuously write and re-write data. The External Events Utility (EEU) that AMD installs alongside its CPU and GPU drivers is reportedly the culprit.

Also: Nvidia RTX 50 GPUs hit with more price hikes

Fortunately, there are a few workarounds available to avert disaster while AMD works on a more permanent solution.

Reports of the issue first surfaced in July on AMD’s official PC user forum, with one user stating that the External Events Client Module and EEU were constantly writing information to their SSD after installing a Radeon 9060XT graphics card. Subsequent comments on the thread this month confirm that the issue has persisted despite several bug fixes and patch updates, with two users reporting hard numbers for data usage ranging from 0.3 MB/s to as much as 1.5 MB/s.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

This week, Reddit user darklinkpower posted that the AMD Adrenaline Edition desktop application also had the EEU driver bug, using up to 1% of their drive health per month for around 16 months. That might not sound like much, but it can cause catastrophic problems if left unchecked.

AMD seems to be aware of the issue; a company official who goes by AMD_Vik on Reddit commented that it will “hopefully [be] fixed in the next [update].” While there’s little indication of how quickly a permanent, official patch will be pushed to users, there are a few ways you can protect yourself from the bug and prevent your storage drive from collapsing.

This seems to be the most consistent fix for most AMD users reporting issues, but disabling the EEU can cause its own problems, such as disabling AMD FreeSync support or introducing display glitches if you hot-swap screens while your PC is powered on.

The AMD Adrenalin Edition desktop app lets you control how your PC components communicate with one another, and it might be another facet of a complex problem. By allowing your CPU to access your graphics card’s memory, you can temporarily boost performance, but the EEU bug seems to let it and your GPU run rampant, eating up every bit of memory they can find. Changing a few settings within the app may help:

Also: I tried local AI on HP’s Omnibook Ultra

This is a more niche solution that carries its own risk of introducing communication issues between your CPU and GPU, so I only recommend trying this route if disabling the EEU itself doesn’t resolve the issue. AMD’s official fix may be in the works, but without a firm timeline for release, users are left twisting in the wind trying to stop their PCs from hemorrhaging storage capacity.

#3151. You can change Windows settings directly from a search now – how to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview enhances the Search feature so that you can access specific settings right from a search window.

Microsoft has been on a kick lately trying to improve and enhance Windows 11, including sprucing up Search, which is now simpler, cleaner, and friendlier. And there’s another cool trick that Search has up its sleeve: Available in the Beta channel of the latest Windows 11 Insiders Preview, Search will give you access to specific Windows settings and commands. Known as inline actions, this latest skill is designed to help you directly complete certain tasks. That means you no longer need to know exactly where or how to find the setting you need.

Also: Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now

Curious about built-in features such as Dark mode, Bluetooth, screen brightness, Remote Desktop, the Windows clipboard, or Windows Update? Just type the name or phrase in the Search field. The results then display an Open button that you can select to go directly to the related setting.

“A new Windows Search experience built on WinUI 3 is beginning to roll out,” Microsoft said on a web page announcing the latest Insiders build. “It’s faster, more efficient, and features a streamlined design that makes results easier to scan. Inline actions let you quickly complete tasks directly. Turn on dark mode or Bluetooth, adjust your screen brightness, mute your device, or arrange windows from Windows Search.”

I tried this with several different Windows settings, and the results window pointed me to the right screens for tweaking them. Though I know where most Windows settings are located by now, there are still times when I forget how to reach certain ones. This new skill promises to be a time saver whenever I face that challenge.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC

Here’s another handy enhancement. How often do you type a word or term in Windows Search only to misspell it? With the latest update, Search will now better understand what you actually mean and match you with the correct results. Type “drak” instead of “dark,” for example, and you’ll still see the results for Dark mode.

Microsoft promises these latest improvements to Windows Search will continue to be fine-tuned over the next few weeks. And there’s more in the new Preview build.

Ever run into trouble using Windows Hello facial recognition in a dark area? Now, your screen will temporarily brighten up to help you sign in under those conditions. To enable this option, head to Settings, select Account, select Sign-in options, and then click Facial recognition. Turn on the switch for “Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition.”

The latest Insiders build also tweaks features such as Live captions, Gaming, File Explorer, and Microsoft 365 cloud storage.

Also: How I used ChatGPT to talk me through fixing a corrupted gaming PC

To grab this update, you’ll have to join the Windows Insiders Program if you’re not already registered. You can then sign up for the Beta or Experimental channel, either of which will give you access to the new Search skills and other features. Make sure you’re running the Beta Preview Build 26320.9876 or higher. To check, go to Settings, select System, and then click About. The Windows Info section will indicate the build number.

As for regular Windows users not enrolled in the Insiders Program, the new changes should reach you relatively soon. I’d expect them to roll out with the December Patch Tuesday update arriving on December 8, so that Microsoft can squeeze them in before the end of the year.

#3150. Google Fi’s ‘Super Network’ Hops Networks to Keep Your Pixel Phone Connected

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Automatic network switching for Pixel phones could mean fewer mobile dead zones.

Even in areas that seem abundant with overlapping cellular coverage, phones sometimes sputter when you’re looking up information or trying to get directions when your carrier’s signal gets weak. To avoid those annoying interruptions, Google Fi Wireless is rolling out what it’s calling a “super network” feature. It automatically switches your phone between two 5G networks to maintain the best connection.

The new capability works only on Google’s phones, starting with the Pixel 9 and newer Pixel models.

The super network is included free for existing Google Fi customers on all of its plans: Flexible, Unlimited Essentials, Unlimited Standard and Unlimited Premium.

Google says that it’s using “two top 5G networks,” but the company is refusing to reveal which networks those are in the US. Traditionally Google Fi runs on T-Mobile’s network.

The network switching also applies when you’re traveling internationally, and is included in the Unlimited Premium and Flexible plans.

According to a source at Google, the phone will use two eSIM slots to switch between networks, but it will appear to only use a single eSIM on the customer’s phone. A fine-print disclaimer notes that any other eSIMs on your device must be disabled, which is worth knowing for anyone that already uses multiple carriers on a single device.

In addition to the super network news, Google said its Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus feature is available in millions of more locations across the US. If the phone is in an area where cellular is spotty and a compatible Wi-Fi network is nearby, it automatically makes an encrypted connection if the Wi-Fi network is stronger.

Wi-Fi Auto Connect Plus is available on Pixel phones, but is also becoming available on Samsung phones running One UI 9 or later and “select modern Motorola phones.”

#3148. Can you still trust Proton?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The company’s reputation took a major hit two weeks ago, when 404 Media published a detailed report, based on leaked Slack messages and interviews with anonymous insiders. The story detailed a push by Proton CEO Andy Yen to — in his own words — “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity.”

Also: Is your browser’s free VPN enough? I tested 4 against Proton VPN

After one employee proposed spending at least a few days on penetration testing before shipping new code, Yen reportedly said, “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure. Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” According to 404 Media’s account, Yen’s message for Proton engineers was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

After the original story broke, 404 Media posted a follow-up story reporting that the company had canceled its “re-interviews” that were intended to assess how developers were adopting AI. A 404 Media podcast was titled “Proton’s CEO Is Putting AI Before Security.”

Reddit has an especially active Proton community with 345,000 weekly visitors. It quickly filled up with so many comments — the majority of them negative — that moderators created a single megathread to help keep track of the different threads, including pages for general criticism, support of the AI usage, and “leaving your goodbyes.”

Also: Best VPN services 2026: Expert tested and recommended

Given the level of interest, it’s not surprising that Yen chose that forum to post a public message to the community. In it, he apologized for “hurtful” remarks, adding that he’s “determined to do better.”

He also addressed the topic of AI-based security reviews:

But most importantly, I need to categorically state that our use of AI will never be at the expense of security. In the past year, contrary to what has been alleged, actually additional layers of security review have been added to meet the threat posed by hostile AIs scanning Proton’s open source code for vulnerabilities. Fast and secure need not be mutually exclusive. We also leverage AI to find vulnerabilities in our own code before attackers do. Our code is open source, and its security remains open for all to verify. [emphasis in original]

Nothing in the 404 Media reporting demonstrates that Proton weakened its encryption or shipped insecure code because of AI. The damage is different: Yen’s remarks undermined confidence that management will consistently respect the security processes its customers rely on.

In a blog post that Proton shared with ZDNET ahead of its publication today, the company followed up on Yen’s promise to “lift the hood on how we use AI internally at Proton.” The post, titled “How Proton keeps your data secure in the age of AI,” was signed by the Proton Team and emphasizes Proton’s secure architecture, with end-to-end, zero-access encryption:

We do not hold the keys to your emails, files, or passwords, so we cannot read them, and no AI tool can, either. Our documented security governance policies have not changed since June 2024, before AI was even a major factor in our work here, and they all still apply.

On Reddit, Yen said, “AI is here, and it will unquestionably change how software is developed forever, and Proton must also change.” Today’s post clarified that code receives the same checks whether it is written by a human, by an AI agent, or by a combination of both. Every change receives automated security scans but also requires human approval; sensitive changes, such as core cryptography work, require review by specialist teams. Major feature designs are also reviewed for security, dependencies, testing, and deployment plans.

Also: I can access my home PCs remotely for free – no VPN needed

Those policies address the most serious technical concerns raised by the current controversy, although outsiders have no way to know from the policy alone how consistently those safeguards are followed in day-to-day development.

Should a modern software company use AI for security? Proton argues that it can’t afford not to.

Because of AI, attacks that once might have required a nation-state can now be executed by almost anyone. A defender relying on manual processes and hand-crafted tools is bringing a knife to a gunfight. An attacker only needs to find one flaw, while a defender needs to close all of them. AI is the only tool that makes that defense possible. Cybersecurity is an arms race, and the teams working on security at Proton have been some of the earliest adopters of AI, because the safety of your data depends on winning that race.

But that argument doesn’t really address the objection. The current controversy isn’t about whether Proton should use AI to find vulnerabilities; it’s about whether pressure for “AI velocity” can override the judgment of engineers responsible for keeping its products secure.

Proton says it uses AI to review code changes, identify vulnerabilities through continuous security reviews, and monitor an attack surface that has “grown far beyond what unaided humans could monitor.” The company uses its own models alongside non-public cyber models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

The modern software development landscape is torn by two opposing forces. On one side, you have AI-based tools that are routinely finding nightmarish vulnerabilities in existing codebases and then exploiting them immediately. On the other side, you have a global movement that’s skeptical of the benefits of AI and outright opposed to construction of the data centers where they run.

Much of Proton’s growth over the past few years has been the direct result of people trying to escape big tech. So it shouldn’t be a surprise that many of Proton’s customers — at least those who are passionate enough to visit a Reddit forum — are deeply skeptical of anything related to AI.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

In a traditional software company, that realization would have led management to cautiously roll out AI-based features and reveal its AI-centric security strategy more deliberately. That didn’t happen here, obviously. Those blunt remarks from the CEO exposed a management culture that many employees and customers found troubling. It’s difficult to restore trust, both within the workforce and among customers, after that kind of public display of contempt.

Ironically, one of Yen’s comments from the original 404 Media story describes the company’s current dilemma with devastating accuracy.

In a Slack message, Yen told a Proton engineer, “perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.” The implication was that he was urging the employee to lie, or at least shade the truth. In fact, as Yen himself told a random Reddit commenter:

I do not believe perception should be more important than truth. I am stating that unfortunately it often ends up being the case. If you place it into the context in which it was said, it can be understood as, “it doesn’t matter that the truth is that Proton’s PQC implementation is better, this truth is irrelevant as long as it is not perceived to be this way, and we therefore need to correct that perception”

That’s Proton’s challenge now, distilled to its essence. It takes seconds to destroy a reputation. It can take months or years to recover from the perception that the company and its management can no longer be trusted.

Personally, I will continue to use Proton Pass and Proton VPN, both of which are solid, reliable products. But I’ve moved my secondary email accounts (which I had migrated from Gmail to Proton Mail); they’re now running on Fastmail. I had been considering making the switch for a long time, primarily because Proton Mail’s performance has been too slow for my taste. Current events just hastened that switch.

#3147. You Should Download iOS 27.2.1 Now for a Handful of Security Fixes

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

Apple said the update fixes issues that could expose sensitive data.

Apple released iOS 27.2.1 on Monday, the same day the company released the first public beta for the upcoming iOS 27.3. The latest update fixes nine issues on your iPhone, including a couple that could expose your data to malicious actors.

You can download iOS 27.2.1 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

Apple says the update provides bug fixes and security updates for issues on your iPhone, two of which may lead to memory corruption on your device.

Memory corruption happens when a program on your device incorrectly reads, writes or frees up memory. This can cause the program to crash, or it could expose sensitive data to others.

You should update your iPhone as soon as possible. Apple didn’t say that these issues were being actively exploited. However, it’s important to keep the software on your device up to date so you’re better protected against potential security threats.

For more iOS news, here’s what features and bug fixes iOS 27.2 brought to your iPhone. You can also check out our iOS 27 cheat sheet for more.
