#3146. Evolution Petroleum (EPM) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Asset sales and a new Permian deal are shaping debt reduction and buyback plans.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Evolution Petroleum Corporation (EPM -3.64%) reported fiscal first quarter results that were centered on the integration of its $16 million Permian minerals acquisition and the conversion of nonproducing acreage into cash through farm-outs. Management reported that revenue increased 6% year over year as higher realized commodity prices offset unplanned downtime in legacy working interest assets. The company is prioritizing a capital allocation strategy that emphasizes the growth of high-margin mineral and royalty interests, which do not require company-funded drilling or completion costs. Management stated that near-term financial priorities include utilizing asset monetization proceeds to reduce debt while sustaining the quarterly dividend and evaluating potential share repurchases.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the Evolution Petroleum Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Earnings Release Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Brandi Hudson, Director of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Brandi Hudson: Thank you. Welcome to Evolution Petroleum's Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Earnings Call. I'm joined today by Kelly Loyd, President and Chief Executive Officer; Mark Bunch, Chief Operating Officer; and Ryan Stash, Senior Vice President, Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer. We released our fiscal first quarter 2027 financial results after the market closed yesterday. Please refer to our earnings press release for additional information containing these results. You can access our earnings release in the Investors section of our website. Please note that any statements and information provided in today's call speak only as of today's date, November 11, 2026, and any time-sensitive information may not be accurate at a later date.

Our discussion today will contain forward-looking statements of management's beliefs and assumptions based on currently available information. These forward-looking statements are subject to the risks, assumptions and uncertainties described in our SEC filings. Actual results may differ materially from those expected. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statements. During today's call, we may discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures, including adjusted EBITDA and adjusted net income. Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in our earnings release. Kelly will begin with an overview of the quarter and our strategic priorities. Mark will follow with an operational update, and Ryan will review our financial results and liquidity.

Kelly will then provide closing comments, and the management team will take your questions. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. A webcast replay will be available in the Investors section of our website. With that, I will turn the call over to Kelly.

Kelly Loyd: Thank you, Brandi, and good morning, everyone. There's a lot to talk about this morning, and I'm pleased to say most of it reflects real progress on our strategy. During the quarter, we closed on a $16 million Permian minerals acquisition, expanded our Haynesville and Bossier Shale royalty position in Louisiana. And after quarter end, we continued our strategy of turning undeveloped acreage into cash. Revenue from the quarter was up 6% from a year ago. Production was slightly up from the fourth quarter. Adjusted EBITDA increased from last quarter. And while net income came in at a loss for the quarter, it was due in large part to hedging losses, most of which were noncash.

Beyond just the quarter's headline numbers, we're very excited about the progress we're seeing across important parts of our business, particularly our mineral and royalty portfolio. September production from our newly acquired Permian interest has already exceeded our acquisition expectations and new wells in Louisiana are beginning to contribute just as we expected. We bought these assets for both their existing production and their substantial development potential, which is really beginning to deliver. What makes that development particularly valuable to us is how it is funded. Our operating partners bear the drilling and completion costs, and we receive our share of production without having to make those additional capital commitments.

We also do not bear lifting expenses on these mineral and royalty interests. That means growth in these assets contributes high-margin cash flow without the CapEx associated with working interest development. As these contributions continue to build, it gives us more capacity to strengthen the balance sheet and further support our dividend. Specifically in the Permian, from the effective date of August 20 through September, production averaged approximately 218 barrels of oil equivalent per day, ahead of the 200 to 210 BOE per day we expected. We have sufficient production data to include the results from 21 of the approximately 27 gross wells that operators brought online between closing and September 30.

That September rate does not yet include production from those roughly 6 additional wells that we know are online. In our fiscal second quarter, we expect to benefit from a full quarter of ownership, production from those 6 wells and production from new wells that come online during the quarter. It's exciting to see this level of activity so soon after closing. Our Louisiana interest offer a similar opportunity. Production from our Haynesville and Bossier royalty interest grew approximately 92% from the fourth quarter as operators brought new wells online, very much in line with our expectations. We added a couple of small bolt-ons during the quarter and have continued adding to the position since quarter end.

We've been building this position over time, and we are now seeing this acreage begin to contribute in a meaningful way. We are also looking beyond new production for ways to realize value within the portfolio. We own a great deal of undeveloped acreage with meaningful long-term potential. Like we did in the fourth fiscal quarter when we sold minerals for $3 million that we felt were unlikely to be developed in the next year or 2, we always consider the best path to bring value forward to today across our portfolio, whether that's participating in development through working interest, selling longer-term development prospects or farming out the acreage to a partner, we have many ways to accelerate value.

In the right situations and where the operator is aligned with us, a farmout of working interest with an override and/or an option to participate can be the most efficient option. It allows us to bring in cash today and retain an interest in future production with 0 CapEx net to us. Following quarter end, we did farm out some undeveloped acreage in the Williston Basin for approximately $2.5 million while retaining a 0.25% overriding royalty interest. This acreage represents roughly 2% of our roughly 40,000 acre position and just a fraction of the 300-plus probable and possible drilling locations that we have identified.

We're also in negotiations for further farm-outs of very low or noncurrently producing acreage here and in other parts of our portfolio that we hope to be able to report on soon. These agreements are expected to generate cash upfront and overrides and possible options to participate, and we intend to apply these proceeds to pay down borrowings on our revolver. That gives us a way to reduce debt while keeping today's production and cash flow fully intact. We expect to find more opportunities like these as we work to strengthen the balance sheet and create value for our shareholders while maintaining future upside. Taken together, these opportunities shape how we are allocating capital.

We've already invested in assets that can contribute more as they develop, and our near-term priority is to realize those returns in the quarters and years ahead. With meaningful growth already built into the portfolio, we can be highly selective about new capital and put more of the cash we generate towards strengthening the balance sheet. That approach also supports our dividend. The Board has declared a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, our 53rd consecutive quarterly payment. And since December 2013, we've returned approximately $156.6 million to shareholders. When we think about that commitment over multiple years and across commodity cycles -- and the growth underway in our mineral and royalty portfolio strengthens our ability to support it.

For fiscal 2007 7, we're off to a start that really reflects the portfolio we've been building, new production from our Permian and Louisiana interest, value emerging from undeveloped acreage and a clear path to stronger cash generation. We look forward to updating you on that progress next quarter. With that, I'll turn the call over to Mark for more details on our operations.

J. Bunch: Thanks, Kelly. Good morning, everyone. I'll focus on the development activity and operating performance across our portfolio and what we see as we move through fiscal 2027. Overall, first quarter operating performance was up sequentially. Underneath that, the picture varies by area. So let me take them in turn, starting with SCOOP/STACK. At SCOOP/STACK, new well activity continued across both our working interest and mineral and royalty positions. During the quarter, 2 gross wells came online, 8 gross wells were in progress, and we elected to participate in 3 additional gross wells. In Louisiana, new wells continue to come online across our Haynesville and Bossier mineral and royalty interest.

During the quarter, we acquired approximately $300,000 of additional interest, primarily in undeveloped acreage that third-party operators are actively developing. That activity continues to build our production without requiring us to fund drilling or completion costs. In the Permian, integration is progressing well. As Kelly mentioned, operators moved at least 21 gross wells into producing status between closing and September 30. With additional wells entering production and a full quarter of ownership, we expect a larger contribution in the second quarter. For now, our Permian and Louisiana volumes are reported within TexMex and other -- and as they become more established in our reporting, we plan to present their contributions separately.

At TexMex, operating costs declined compared to the year ago quarter following the change of operator. In the Barnett Shale, we have met with the new operator whose entire focus is solely on Barnett operations and improving field profitability through operating changes and workover opportunities. At Delhi, oil production was affected by continued compressor downtime during the quarter. Finally, at Chaveroo, we continue to work with our partner on the timing of future drilling. We view the development inventory as attractive, particularly in the current price environment, and we'll provide updates as plans develop. With that, I will turn it over to Ryan.

Ryan Stash: Thanks, Mark, and good morning. As Brandi mentioned earlier, we issued our earnings release yesterday, which contains more information on our results. For today, I'd like to go through our fiscal first quarter financial highlights. In fiscal Q1, production averaged 6,978 BOE per day, up 1% sequentially and down 5% year-over-year. The lower year-over-year production was due to unplanned downtime at our Delhi and TexMex assets as well as natural declines across the portfolio. In addition, the prior year period includes flush production from wells brought online at Chaveroo Field. These declines were partially offset by development in our SCOOP/STACK asset as well as mineral and royalty acquisitions in the Haynesville/Bossier Shale and Permian.

Total revenues were $22.6 million, down 7% sequentially and up 6% year-over-year. The sequential decrease reflected lower realized oil and NGL prices, partially offset by higher natural gas realizations and increased production. Compared to the year ago quarter, average realized prices before hedge settlements increased 11%, more than offsetting the decline in production. Net loss for the quarter was $3 million or $0.08 per diluted share compared to net income of $4.6 million in fiscal Q4 and net income of $0.8 million or $0.02 per diluted share in the year ago period. The quarter included a $4.1 million unrealized loss on derivative contracts compared to a $5.8 million unrealized gain in fiscal Q4.

Excluding selected items, adjusted net loss narrowed to $0.3 million from $0.6 million sequentially compared to an adjusted net loss of $0.1 million a year ago. Adjusted EBITDA increased sequentially to $6.8 million, driven by lower operating costs as a result of increased mineral and royalty production that helped offset lower revenues. Compared to the prior year quarter, adjusted EBITDA declined from $7.3 million, primarily due to lower production and lower realized natural gas prices compared to the prior year period. Lease operating costs decreased to $12.4 million compared to $13.1 million in the year ago quarter.

The decrease was primarily driven by lower operating costs at SCOOP/STACK and at TexMex following the change of operator as well as lower taxes and gathering and transportation costs associated with decreased natural gas prices at Jonah and Barnett. On a per unit basis, LOE per BOE improved approximately 1% from the year ago quarter and improved approximately 5% sequentially to $19.25 from $20.35 in fiscal Q4. On the hedging front, we have continued to add hedges to comply with our credit facility covenants. Our ongoing goal remains to reduce commodity price risk and protect cash flow for our shareholder return strategy while preserving the maximum potential upside.

This strategy can result in realized and unrealized losses on our hedges in some periods, but benefit us in other periods and provide more predictable and stable cash flows over time. Currently, we have hedged approximately 73% of expected PDP oil production and 76% of expected PDP natural gas production for the remainder of calendar year 2026. For calendar year 2027, we have hedged approximately 72% of expected PDP oil production and 67% of expected PDP natural gas production. Volumes for 100% of our NGL production and development on our asset base remains unhedged to provide upside to commodity pricing. We continue to utilize a mix of swaps and collars to hedge both oil and gas.

For the quarter, realized losses on our derivative contracts were $1.3 million compared to realized gains of $0.9 million a year ago. That change reduced adjusted EBITDA by approximately $2.2 million year-over-year. The volumes and prices by instrument and period are included in the hedge schedule in our earnings release. Turning to the balance sheet. Cash on hand totaled $3.1 million at September 30, down from $6.1 million at June 30. Borrowings under our credit facility increased during the quarter to $60 million from $56.5 million as a result of the Permian Minerals acquisition with $0.8 million in letters of credit outstanding and a weighted average interest rate of 6.48%.

Total liquidity at September 30, including cash and available borrowing capacity was approximately $15.3 million. We generated $8.4 million in operating cash flow before changes in working capital during the quarter compared to $6.5 million in fiscal Q4. Capital expenditures incurred were $0.7 million, and we completed the $16 million Permian Minerals acquisition. We also received approximately $12.5 million of net proceeds from our common stock offering and had $3.5 million of net borrowings under our credit facility.

Subsequent to quarter end, our borrowing base was redetermined at $70 million, down from the interim $73 million borrowing base established in August to provide liquidity to complete the Permian Minerals acquisition, but up from the spring 2026 borrowing base value of $65 million. As of October 20, availability on the facility was $9.2 million. This does not include approximately $2.5 million in cash received for the closing of the initial Williston farm-out transaction in November or any subsequent farm-out transactions that we're currently pursuing. During the quarter, we paid $4.9 million in common stock dividends.

The Board has declared a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share for fiscal Q2 2027, payable December 31 to shareholders of record on December 15, marking our 53rd consecutive quarterly payment. As we move through fiscal 2027, our financial priorities remain focused on maintaining liquidity, managing leverage and deploying capital where we expect attractive returns per share. The growing contribution from our recent mineral and royalty investments that don't require any CapEx, combined with expected farm-out proceeds support our focus on reducing borrowings while continuing to return capital to shareholders. I'll now hand it back over to Kelly for closing comments.

Kelly Loyd: Thanks, Ryan. As we move through fiscal '27, our focus is on realizing the returns from the portfolio that we have already built. We're encouraged by the early performance of our recent investments and the opportunities ahead, while recognizing that the measure of our progress will be the cash those assets generate for shareholders. We will remain disciplined in how we commit capital with debt reduction and sustaining our quarterly dividend at the forefront of our decisions. We appreciate your continued support of Evolution and look forward to updating you on our progress. I just want to say thank you and Happy Veterans Day to all of our bests out there.

With that, I'll turn it back over to the operator to begin the Q&A session.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question today comes from Jeff Grampp with Northland Capital Markets.

Jeffrey Grampp: I want to start on the Permian. I know it's super early here, but just curious how the performance thus far has been relative to the underwriting model. I know you guys were expecting that asset to grow, and it seems like that's playing out. But just kind of curious how that's tracking in early days. And if you have a rig count on the assets, that would be interesting as well.

J. Bunch: So Jeff, it's Mark Bunch. And so far, like at the rate we're converting, it'd be almost like we'd be converting it around 200 wells per year. So we're actually really quite happy because we actually didn't underwrite on anything that large. And I'll let Ryan answer the question about the rig count.

Ryan Stash: Yes. So we're still -- Jeff, we're still running 8 rigs currently out there. Double Eagle has got 4. Exxon's got 4. The other interesting thing is even since the end of the quarter, we've seen upwards of 30 to 40 permits actually been filed here since the end of the quarter. Diamondback actually filed some new ones on our acreage here in the last couple of weeks. And Apache still got a few out there. So we definitely think even beyond Double Eagle and Exxon, there should be some other guys moving rigs in soon.

Kelly Loyd: Yes. Jeff, this is Kelly. I mean one of the things, right, we only want to include production that we actually know, right? So we got information on 21 wells that were converted. We have another 6 that we know are on production, but we didn't have information on. So we couldn't include any results from those. So that 218 could be a little understated, frankly.

Jeffrey Grampp: That all sounds really good. I appreciate the details. For my follow-up, kind of a bigger picture question. You just have a slide in the new deck, I think kind of targeting like 20% pro forma cash flow coming from minerals and royalties. Just kind of curious, like based on this quarter's results or maybe looking forward a couple of quarters, like where does that trend over time given that the royalty stuff seems to be the faster growing of the asset base today?

Kelly Loyd: Yes. And you sort of put the nail on the head. You said today, right? So as we currently speak, I do think we continue to see some highly accretive opportunities there. So look, just naturally, with a couple of the assets that's growing and a couple of having natural declines, it should grow just on its own without us doing anything else. So we do see that growing over time. But also, look, with where we are right now, the competition for dollars to pay down debt, we'll talk to the Board about maybe even a share buyback, it gets pretty stiff. So any new acquisition is going to have to look really good.

Ryan Stash: Yes, Jeff, I don't think -- the 20% number, I think, obviously, we still feel good about, and we're probably close to that. Obviously, going forward, some of it is going to depend on performance of legacy assets versus drilling pace in the Permian, right? So we still think kind of that 20% number right now kind of makes sense, but obviously, something to change as we see how the other assets perform.

Operator: The next question comes from Jeff Robertson with Water Tower Research.

Jeffrey Robertson: Kelly, to follow on your previous discussion, from a high-level perspective, how much exposure or organic growth exposure do you think the minerals portfolio gives to help offset natural declines on the legacy non-op working interest assets and again, with the minerals interest adding volumes at 0 CapEx and virtually 0 LOE?

Kelly Loyd: Right. Well, we -- if you model it out in a static sense, it gets a large part of the way there. I don't know that it gets all the way there. A lot of it will depend on are we starting from this level with the legacy assets and the working interest assets and what they produce and how are they going to perform. So it's -- a couple of the assets didn't perform as we might have wanted. We think we have some real fixes in -- certainly in the TexMex area. And with Delhi sort of remains to be seen with more compressors were down during the quarter.

And so you just don't know what exactly it's going to do from there. But I think overall, we're pretty excited, and it goes a long way towards holding production flat without any additional CapEx.

Ryan Stash: Yes. I mean I think as we've said in the past, I mean, given the delta on production from buying royalty assets versus working interest, just where we sit today, you could see production decline some, but cash flow is going to remain pretty strong, right? So obviously, depending on strip, we do think that the addition of the assets can certainly go a long way to replacing the cash flow loss from decline in our legacy assets.

J. Bunch: Right. That's more how we look at it really is what is the cash it's going to produce.

Jeffrey Robertson: On the Williston farm-out, did the operator give any indication of their commitment toward drilling the wells that they purchase?

Kelly Loyd: Yes, the new operator, yes, they have actually have to have -- it's written such that they're required for a drilling commitment. So yes, everything is -- that well is on their drilling schedule. Jeff, I'm glad you brought that up. I mean that's something we're really excited about. If you recall, when we first bought this, there were 350-ish plus identified locations that were probable, possible sticks on a piece of paper. But for the right sort of drilling cost and for the right commodity price environment, those are very real possibilities.

And a bigger company with a continuous drilling program that can get these drilled at much more efficient cost than we and our small partner up there, they start to make a whole lot of sense. And we've seen activity, as we mentioned in the past, moving towards us. And it's allowed us to be part of a bigger group here and retain that override as well as get some cash upfront. And I think we alluded to this, we have 40,000 acres in that area. This was 636 -- and I'm excited to see what comes down the pipe as the activity and results come in. And we're talking to others that have approached us.

And to the point, like as we make other deals in the future here, they'll always have a drilling commitment associated with them, especially if we have like an override because obviously, why would you keep an override if you didn't sell out and had no recourse. So there's always going to be some sort of drilling commitment when we make one of these farm-out deals.

Jeffrey Robertson: So you can convert long-dated drilling development activity into the mineral and royalty portfolio after they drill the wells and you collect on your overrides?

Kelly Loyd: Yes. And also just allows for the fact that we're not completely selling out of our acreage. If they, for some reason, like not to drill or perform, then our acreage comes back to us. But we just don't want to disappear. We want to -- we only want it to become -- shall we say like it convert to an override if the case is they actually perform and drill wells.

Jeffrey Robertson: In the Barnett market, have the conversations with the new operators started to lead to any proposals on activity? And do you think that there will be CapEx dollars spent in that area in 2027?

Kelly Loyd: I don't know about the CapEx side, but they've already approached us about wanting to do some additional workovers. I think they've already put some online in some of the areas that were more struggling economically. So -- and they've gone into some of the areas and looked at reducing costs. So yes, we're actually really happy with the way the new operator is performing.

Jeffrey Robertson: And then lastly, Ryan, on the RBL with the $70 million borrowing base and the Williston deal, it sounds like you were able to create liquidity without having any impact on the collateral value for the borrowing base since these are undeveloped locations that you've essentially farmed down and converted to an overriding cash.

Ryan Stash: Yes, that's exactly right. In fact, I think some of the ones specifically in the Williston were actually mortgage because they were just -- it was just acreage and PUDs. And to the extent that we do the same thing, I think it's going to be the same going forward, right? So we're going to be selling very little, if any, PDP or production, right, mostly just acreage or PUDs, which won't impact the borrowing base. And it could be that the cash you get upfront is worth more than the PUDs are on the books for, right?

Operator: The next question comes from Nicholas Pope with ROTH Capital.

Nicholas Pope: I was hoping we could expand a little bit on Jeff's question on potential CapEx here in fiscal '27. As you look at some of the deals with bigger working interest where maybe spending has been a little light for the last year or so. Is there any visibility into Chaveroo, SCOOP/STACK? Like I'm just trying to broaden a little bit an understanding of what might be on kind of the -- what potential might be out there to kind of increase CapEx the remainder of fiscal '27?

Kelly Loyd: Yes. So what I'd say as far as -- we'll start with SCOOP/STACK working interest. That is kind of -- we have not seen anything that would make us change sort of our current -- the way it's looked in the past. We expect it to be similar to that. And the AFEs are sort of coming in, in line with our -- the way it has the last year or so. So I think we're kind of on pace there. And as for Chaveroo, like I said, we're excited about those. We think those wells make nice returns right now. And I'll just say we're still working with the operator on scheduling when, if, timing, all that on those.

We have some permitted wells that we think are going to have really nice returns, but we're working with the operator on that. As you know, they've had a small shake up there.

Nicholas Pope: I'll make sure to ask them about it as well tomorrow on their call. Curious, sustainability of kind of where operating costs have been running. We've seen a couple of quarters of pretty decent improvement in kind of unit operating costs. Just trying to understand a little bit how much of that might be the mix changing with more royalty interest versus some more, I guess, sustainable or longer-term kind of improvements in that -- seeing that lower operating costs across the board. Like where is that coming from? Should we expect kind of the rate that we're seeing right now to be sustained over the next year?

Ryan Stash: Yes. I mean, Nick, it's Ryan. I would expect -- in fact, we hope the rate will actually come down from what we reported, right? I mean we should continue to see some improvements, as we've mentioned, sort of in TexMex as wells have come online and the operator gets to hold kind of the asset. And then as you mentioned, certainly, the royalty production having such low LOE in the $2 to $3 per BOE range compared to kind of our other assets as that becomes a bigger piece, that's certainly going to take the LOE down.

So yes, I mean, I think we were like around, what, mid- $19, above $19 per BOE, and we do think that, that level should come down over time.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The next question comes from Poe Fratt with Alliance Global Partners.

Charles Fratt: I have 2 questions. The first of which is you're talking about additional farm-outs raising capital. Can you sort of frame the potential proceeds from those farm-outs, $5.5 million over the last 2 quarters roughly. What should we -- any way to frame what the future might hold there?

Kelly Loyd: Well, I'll play this a little closer to the best because we are in talks with a few parties right now. But I'll say this. We don't want to do everything all at once because we think as results come in, it will translate into higher value later on. But you do want to do enough to get that increased activity by the bigger operators who can drill these things as part of a continuous drilling program and be super-efficient. So be a little bit of a balance there. And by the way, we're also -- it's not just Williston. We have other areas where people have approached us, too.

So I would say, hopefully, we'll have something here we can announce pretty soon that will at least clear up your immediate-term question.

Charles Fratt: And -- when you talked about stock buybacks, Kelly, it's ironic because you just issued stock for an acquisition. But what -- is there anything within your credit agreements that's holding you back here? I mean the stock is just getting crushed. And I was just wondering sort of how you're thinking about that and whether there are any structural issues that you have to contend with?

Ryan Stash: No, there's nothing from a structural issue perspective, Poe, I mean, obviously, yes, I mean we did issue stock to get the Permian deal done. But we've also announced and as you kind of asked the question, we've had some additional proceeds come in from accelerating asset sales. So when we have that cash come in, we have the options of obviously paying down debt, which may be the initial use of proceeds, but we'll also look at making investments and where our stock -- I agree with you. I think the reaction is overdone today.

But where it's trading, I mean, it's maybe buying our stock back could be our best investment of capital right now to look at creating shareholder value. So as we -- again, as we monetize some of the portfolio and rationalize the asset base, one of the use of proceeds could be potentially buying back shares, and there's nothing prohibited in our credit agreement for that.

Charles Fratt: And then just if I may, just one more. Delhi, what's the color on that? It seems to have been a thorn in your side for an extended period of time. And can you just sort of preview what the next couple of quarters look like there?

J. Bunch: Well, yes, this is Mark Bunch. So we've been advised by the operator that one of the compressors is not running. They haven't told us when they're going to have it back up and running. And what that amounts to is that they had to shut in some production in order to not have excess CO2 that they would have to flare. So we don't know from the operator when that particular metric is going to change on how they're operating the field. We're trying to figure that out when we know that. And we have better color on that, we'll let you know.

Kelly Loyd: That compressor issue led to the step down in production this quarter. So we hope that changes and gets better, but it's already down.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over for any closing remarks.

Kelly Loyd: No, I just want to thank everyone for joining us here, and that's it. Thank you.

Operator: The conference has now concluded. Thank you for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect.

#3145. Top Wall Street analysts recommend these 3 dividend stocks for solid returns

Global stock markets remain volatile amid uncertainty in the Middle East and a focus on artificial intelligence stocks. Investors seeking steady income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend stocks with attractive yields.

Top Wall Street analysts can help pick stocks that pay regular dividends while having the ability to generate capital appreciation and boost total returns.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Viper Energy is a subsidiary of Diamondback Energy and is focused on owning and acquiring mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. For Q1 2026, the company declared a base dividend of 38 cents per share and a variable dividend of 30 cents per share. VNOM offers a dividend yield of 5%.

Recently, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold initiated coverage of Viper Energy stock with a buy rating and a price target of $58. "The company is advantaged given its scale, core Permian focus, inventory duration, and aligned operating partner," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst highlighted that Viper's Permian-focused asset base and significant scale relative to peers position it as a best-in-class operator. Hanold added that VNOM's 75% liquids-weighted production mix offers meaningful leverage in a strong oil price environment.

Additionally, Hanold projects Viper's inventory life at 15 to 20 years, considering the current development pace of its operating partners, which is significantly higher than that of peers. Among the other advantages, the analyst highlighted VNOM's relationship with Diamondback Energy, which has about a 39% ownership in the company. Hanold said Viper's relationship with Diamondback gives it an edge over its peers, given that it provides visibility into forward activity and production, high-margin organic growth, and steady revenue and cash flows.

Finally, Hanold highlighted Viper's solid balance sheet. He noted that the company is investment-grade rated and has a lower cost of capital, which would support sustainable distributions and strategic mergers and acquisitions. The analyst also emphasized VNOM's attractive capital returns framework.

Hanold ranks No. 152 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 20.2%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Hanold is also bullish on independent oil and natural gas company, Permian Resources. He has a buy rating on PR stock with a price target of $27. Permian announced a base dividend of 16 cents per share for the second quarter of 2026. PR stock offers a dividend yield of 3.2%.

In a recent research note, Hanold updated his estimates for Permian Resources, Devon Energy, and Matador Resources to reflect the impact of the acquisition of undeveloped acres in the New Mexico Delaware Basin by these companies under the federal lease sale. While Devon and Matador spent $2.6 billion and $1.1 billion, respectively, Permian spent $152 million on 6,634 acres and added 50-60 net locations.

Specifically, Hanold noted that $152 million spent by Permian equates to almost one quarter of drilling, based on this year's pace. He added that the transaction aligns with Permian Resources' quarterly acquisition activity and was funded with available cash.

The analyst expects PR stock to outperform its peer group over the next 12 months. He expects Permian Resources to generate peer-leading free cash flow yields, supporting a solid shareholder-return strategy.

"The company has large, contiguous acreage positions in the core of the southern and northern Delaware Permian with a 12-15 year inventory alongside a sizable position in the southern Midland Permian," highlighted Hanold. See Permian Resources Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Finally, let's look at oil and gas giant, Chevron. The company returned $6 billion of cash to shareholders in the first quarter, including $2.5 billion via share repurchases and $3.5 billion in dividends. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share, CVX stock offers a dividend yield of 3.8%.

Recently, Mizuho analyst Nitin Kumar reaffirmed a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $230. The analyst raised his 2026 and 2027 oil price projections, as he expects the impact of the U.S.-Iran conflict on oil prices and refining cracks to persist longer than its effect on Nymex crude prices.

Kumar highlighted that, despite a more constructive macro outlook on oil, large-cap oil-focused exploration and production companies, U.S. refiners, and integrated oil companies are all trading below the average price-to-net-asset-value range from the past 15-plus years. The analyst said that his ratings for the upstream and IOC segments already reflect this "value" opportunity in Chevron, ConocoPhillips, Devon, Diamondback and Occidental Petroleum stocks.

Meanwhile, the five-star analyst noted that the major debate surrounding Chevron centers on inventory depth and whether the company can sustain upstream volumes over the long term without sacrificing capital efficiencies. In this regard, Kumar highlighted that management has shifted its focus away from growth spending toward maximizing free cash flow.

Also, Kumar thinks that improved well productivity in the Permian Basin, including the use of surfactants, has alleviated some investor concerns and increased confidence in CVX's plan to sustain plateau production of more than 1 mmboe/d from the basin through the end of the next decade. Among other positives, Kumar listed the Hess acquisition, which adds a top-quality deepwater asset, recent investments in lithium and power businesses, and "a strong track record of delivering cash returns for shareholders."

Kumar ranks No. 1,098 among more than 12,200 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 7.2%. See Chevron Financials on TipRanks.

#3144. How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain – and what you can do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

New research provides a stark look at the AI supply chain and the risks it brings to businesses.

Artificial intelligence companies worldwide are bringing a new wave of vulnerabilities and security issues to the digital supply chain, researchers warn.

According to a new report published by Black Kite on Tuesday, there now exists a “widespread cybersecurity weakness” across the “rapidly expanding ecosystem of companies developing, deploying, and supporting artificial intelligence.”

AI and smart solutions don’t automatically equate with safe solutions. In a study titled “2026 AI Supply Chain Report: The Risks Behind Your AI Relationships,” Black Kite says that many AI suppliers — the companies that develop and deploy AI services to today’s businesses — are struggling with “basic security practices.”

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

According to the research, after examining the companies themselves, along with their software, integrations, and components, researchers found failures to patch critical vulnerabilities, protect credentials, authenticate users and email, and address network security issues.

The study analyzes 18,160 AI companies worldwide, ranging from 0-10 employees to more than 1,000 employees. A company’s AI involvement was determined through reviews of company products and services and primary business activities, covering six broad groups: everyday application development; AI development and implementation; AI applications in specialized sectors such as healthcare, IT, and finance; industrial organizations; and AI foundations working on data, compute, and modeling.

A small percentage of assessed companies are considered “unclassified,” and the study excluded businesses that use AI only incidentally.

In addition, unusual network activity was detected at 44.3% of organizations, and botnet-related activity was recorded at 41.8% of AI companies.

AI’s main business appeal is its ability to integrate with existing software and platforms to handle manual tasks, heavy lifting, and tedious, time-consuming work, freeing employees to focus on work that requires human oversight.

Enterprises are investing billions of dollars in AI. Menlo’s 2026 research estimates that enterprise AI spend reached $37 billion in 2025, with half of overall spend going to AI apps. In total, 76% of enterprise AI solutions are purchased rather than built internally.

However, the moment an AI or automated component is introduced into a corporate ecosystem or operational platform, any security problems it has impact the user — and each additional integration, such as software components or open-source tooling, may also increase the attack surface.

In an accompanying analysis of AI firms’ use of Model Context Protocol (MCP) components, which can link AI apps to business systems, 48.8% of 1,732 logged security findings were rated High or Critical, including code and command injection vulnerabilities.

Also: The new enterprise AI expert every company needs

It’s not just the AI application itself. As noted by Black Kite, AI suppliers often have access to customer data, developer environments, business infrastructure, and enterprise platforms. If the supplier’s credentials are stolen, this could expose its customers to a range of cyberattacks.

The researchers found, for example, that 19.9% of AI companies offering solutions for enterprise AI deployment had corporate login information in infostealer records, and that stolen corporate logins, overall, were linked to 6.8% of AI suppliers in the study.

Visibility matters, too, for businesses that should be monitoring their digital supply chains. However, 33.2% of AI companies assessed have a “limited” digital footprint, including their domains, subdomains, and IP addresses.

The same principles for protecting the digital supply chain apply to AI suppliers, where continual monitoring and assessment are among the best protections businesses have.

Staying informed and aware of the risks to your own business makes all the difference. As recommended by Black Kite, it takes more than a single point-in-time security assessment — frequent monitoring and engaging with suppliers to understand their technologies and dependencies can reveal potential security issues.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance?

If you find weaknesses, manage them by priority, handling ransomware-related exposures and vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild first.

Also audit an AI tool’s integrations and components, access, what data it can reach, and the potential impact of exploitation. Once you’re armed with this information, it’s possible to weigh risk and reward — and whether the AI tool is worth the potential attack exposure it brings. If you decide to keep it, limit its permissions and access to what it requires.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google has spent the past year making Gemini smarter, more capable and better connected to the apps and services people use every day. But one of its most useful features might also be one of its most personal: memory.

As Gemini has evolved, it's gotten better at remembering details from previous conversations, picking up where you left off and helping with ongoing projects. That's convenient, especially if you use the chatbot regularly, but it also raises an important question: How much does Gemini actually remember about you?

Until now, managing Gemini's memory hasn't always been straightforward. Google has offered controls for reviewing and deleting chat activity, but understanding what the chatbot has learned about you is another matter.

That's where Gemini's new Memory summary comes in. The feature gives users a clearer look at the information Gemini remembers about them, along with the ability to make changes.

Here's how to find your Memory summary, see what Gemini remembers and take control of the information it uses to personalize your conversations.

Google has begun rolling out its new “Memory summary” feature in Gemini for users who work with the chatbot through its desktop and mobile browser versions (it doesn’t seem to be working with the mobile Gemini app at the moment, however). And with this update comes the ability for users to take a look at what Gemini remembers about them and edit it to add more details about themselves or delete it as a whole.

The Memory summary doesn’t just feature a massive info dump that’s all about you—it actually summarizes everything it remembers about you via bullet points that detail your background, relationships, work, interests and preferences. After observing everything Gemini has learned about you and retained as the data it has gained from your previous conversations.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

I actually used my personal Gemini account to see how this new feature works. Accessing it on desktop and through your mobile browser is as simple as going to your “Settings” and clicking on “Personal Intelligence” to be led to the “Memory” and “Memory summary” tabs. You can toggle the Memory tab to let Gemini keep retaining information about you or stop it from performing that action. I clicked on the Memory summary tab and this is the summarized information it has collected about me so far (I’ll be sure to add more information about my profession at some point):

Google has stated that the Memory feature is only available to Gemini users in the US who are over the age of 18 and have an active Google AI plan. Also, those users must have the “Keep activity” and “Memory” options enabled. But in my case, I got to play around with the Memory feature through my free Gemini subscription plan.

AI users have already gotten hip to the fact that most chatbots can bring up past details from their past conversations and use that information to generate more personalized answers to their questions & prompts. It’s nice to see Google allow Gemini users to not only get a full picture of what its chatbot has learned and remembered about them, but also give those same users the opportunity to add, change or delete those details.

Elton Jones covers AI for Tom’s Guide, and tests all the latest models, from ChatGPT to Gemini to Claude to see which tools perform best — and how they can improve everyday productivity.

#3141. Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep an eye on things – even upstairs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Alongside the Ring Drone Cam, Ring introduced the Rover Cam for businesses. It investigates disturbances and streams 4K footage.

Today, Ring announced the launch of a new subbrand, Ring Robotics, with two new products: the $249 Ring Drone Cam, an indoor “mobile security camera” drone that shoots 2K video, and the $999 Ring Rover Cam, a security robot for businesses that patrols autonomously and investigates disturbances.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Studio gives Alexa+ an AI camera to see inside your home

Both devices use Ring’s custom navigation software, “AI Pilot,” to autonomously navigate interior spaces and move between set points along a patrol, rather than being controlled directly by the user. AI Pilot leverages the devices’ cameras, sensors, and vision models, along with cloud processing, to create interior maps, then move the devices between predesignated patrol points such as a side door or a window.

I recently saw both new robots in person at a showcase in New York hosted by Ring’s founder and chief inventor, Jamie Siminoff. They certainly do what they advertise but come with some significant limitations. The drone, for example, can only stay in the air for about 8 minutes before it needs to dock and recharge, while the Ring Rover Cam is slow and deliberate, seemingly ideal for routine surveillance rather than rapid response to an event.

The Ring Drone Cam moves around predetermined patrol points in your home, sending you a live 2K video feed whether you’re just in another room or out of town. The user doesn’t actually fly the drone; instead, it moves around autonomously using Ring’s custom “AI Pilot” navigation technology, leveraging its cameras, sensors, and cloud processing to create a map of its surroundings. This allows it to fly through the air at an appropriate height, going from room to room, even up stairs.

In the Ring app, the user creates patrol points they want the drone to move between — likely a window, doorway, or high-traffic room — creating a set path that is both predictable (so you always know where the drone will go) and relevant, so it’s only monitoring the areas you want it to. But here is where its limitations come into play: It needs a finite path to navigate because its flight time is limited to just five to eight minutes in the air before it has to return to its charging dock.

That makes the dock both the start and end point for the drone’s routine trips, and it’s designed with this in mind. When it goes to land, the drone hovers over the dock and lowers itself down, dropping into place so it can start charging automatically. I asked about its potential to land elsewhere, and Ring told me it would only make an emergency landing outside of its dock in case it didn’t have enough power to get home.

Also: Amazon’s new Echo Dot can turn into a Wi-Fi extender – how it works

There’s one other very important caveat: This thing is loud. There’s no sneaking up on anyone with the Ring Drone Cam, as the entire household is likely to hear it the second it undocks. The four propellers emit a constant, high-pitched whirring while in the air that’s loud enough to announce its presence to anyone in the vicinity: intruder or resident.

During the product briefing, Siminoff insinuated that this was part of its design to dissuade home intruders snooping around your house at night (especially when paired with the drone’s front-facing spotlight), but it’s likely just the result of its engineering, especially considering this is a first-gen product. It’s so loud that it makes me think it’s better suited to navigating the home when no one’s home (although whether or not your pets go bonkers trying to catch it is a whole other issue).

The Ring Drone is designed to work out of the box with the existing Ring ecosystem, including the 2K Video Doorbell and Indoor Cam, and is also compatible with Amazon’s Map View.

The Ring Drone Cam will start shipping on Jan. 27, 2027, and will cost $249.

The other product Ring announced is the Rover Cam, a mobile robot with a 4K camera designed to monitor large spaces like warehouses, offices, or businesses. Ring calls it a “security guard that never clocks out,” but it’s more like a slow-moving droid that goes on set patrol paths. It leverages the same AI Pilot technology as the Ring Drone to map its surroundings and navigate around shelving, furniture, and obstacles in real time.

It’s much quieter than its airborne sibling, traveling at low speeds and offering mobile surveillance instead of wiring every square inch of a large space. If the technology here looks familiar, it’s because it resembles the Amazon Astra, a smaller robot designed for home monitoring but with a very similar build.

The idea here is to deploy the robot to certain areas of a workplace via the app, then get 360-degree views once it’s there. Like the drone, it can also set out on automated routes at select timing intervals — like right after a business closes or before it opens. During working hours, it chugs along with its camera, capturing everything in its view.

Also: The 4 biggest Amazon smart home announcements from today

If another Ring device is triggered, the Rover Cam autonomously goes to investigate the disturbance, providing 4K footage in real time via the app. It also features a periscope camera that can extend to see over obstacles like shelving, counters, or furniture, providing a high-level view if needed. In case you lose it in a large warehouse or office, it has a “light tower” that projects light upward onto the ceiling, notifying users of its location.

Even when docked, it uses motion-sensing technology to start recording the second it senses any kind of movement, just like Ring doorbell cameras. In case of an emergency, the Rover features a siren and red flashing lights to dissuade intruders.

The Ring Rover Cam is available for preorder now and will start shipping on Dec. 16, 2026. It will cost $999.

Management acquired Neurotech Pharmaceuticals to secure ENCELTO, an encapsulated cell therapy surgically implanted into the eye to treat Macular Telangiectasia Type 2, a rare progressive retinal disease causing central vision loss. The product targets an estimated pool of 25,000 diagnosed U.S. patients and offers projected peak sales between $250 million to $400 million.

Aggregate eye care market growth sits at 3%, and commercial execution remains focused on outpacing baseline demand. High equipment penetration and premium product trade-ups support structural growth while executive teams watch price realization and operational efficiency.

Operational savings of $130 million reinforce margin leverage as revenue expansion outpaces baseline expenses.

#3139. Google Introduces 3 More Top-Level Domain Names, Including .Eat and .Fly

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Prospective website owners can now register domains geared toward food, travel and local bands.

We’re trained to type .com almost on autopilot, but more top-level domains are coming. You’ll soon see websites ending in .eat, .fly and .here. It’s a new way for restaurants, travel agencies and other service providers to customize their online presence.

Google successfully filed these domain types with ICANN, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, back in 2012, but only released the new registry options to the public on Tuesday.

There’s always a concern that someone will steal a business’ domain name, a process known as cybersquatting. To prevent new top-level domains from being registered and ransomed at high prices, Google’s partnered registrars offered .eat, .fly and .here websites to registered trademark holders ahead of a wider rollout. This closed access period lasted from Sept. 1 to Nov. 9.

Google’s blog post about the new domains revealed several big businesses that have already secured new web addresses during the trademark holder selloff. Wingstop bought up wingstop.eat, while agriculture and food-tech company Clayton Farms secured the america.eat address. Caddy, Canary and Voltair are some of the businesses with new .fly domains.

The most interesting assortment of companies have tied down .here addresses. In its blog, Google describes .here domains as denoting businesses “where people get things done.” They utilize fairly common words that people might search for. Real-estate app Zillow owns rent.here and sell.here, while bloodtest.here is owned by SiPhox Health, a home blood-testing service.

A number of Google-partnered registrars are now accepting registrations for the three new domain types.

There’s currently a one-time early registration fee associated with registering the new domain names, though it is diminishing and will completely disappear on Nov. 17. After that, any currently unused .eat, .fly and .here names can be registered and maintained at a fixed annual rate, just like any other type of domain.

A representative for Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

#3138. 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Smart Assistants

With the latest betas for iOS and other platforms, Siri AI is now available to all developers for full integration into their apps. Here are the ones I hope will jump on board.

One of the many benefits of the new Siri AI is its ability to work directly with apps on your device via a feature known as App Intents. Currently, this skill includes many of Apple’s own built-in apps and some third-party ones. But with the latest public and developer betas for iOS 27.3, the company is expanding support to all third-party developers.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade

With App Intents, you’re able to ask Siri to tackle a variety of actions among various built-in and third-party apps. On a basic level, you can tell it to perform tasks such as getting directions, playing music, scheduling meetings, sending messages, adding reminders, and finding photos.

On a more advanced level, you can ask it to do things like organize your inbox, edit a photo, and analyze and help you with your current screen. You could also tell it to combine several actions in one shot, work across multiple apps, and engage in a natural back-and-forth conversation.

Introduced in 2022 with iOS 16, the App Intents skill does play well with classic Siri, no Apple Intelligence required. This applies not just to built-in apps but also to third-party apps. However, classic Siri lacks the AI smarts and advanced skills of the latest version.

Siri AI fully supports most built-in apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It does support some third-party apps, but its more advanced features are limited or unavailable.

That’s the gap the new developer betas aim to close. With iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, MacOS 27.3, and VisionOS 27.3, all developers will be able to use Siri AI to fully support and integrate with their apps. For example, instead of manually opening an app like DoorDash or Grubhub to check or change a food order, you can tell Siri to do it for you.

Also: The Siri AI waitlist is gone in iOS 27: How to try the beta now

“Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, on-screen awareness, natural language, and more,” Apple said in a news release for developers. “So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.”

As I use many third-party apps on my iPhone and iPad, both personally and professionally, I’m looking forward to enhanced support for the ones I rely on. With that in mind, here are five apps for which I’d welcome the new and full Siri AI integration.

I often use Amazon on my iPhone and iPad to shop for and purchase items, review my wishlist, and check the status of products I’ve ordered. To do any of those things, I have to open the app and manually go to the right screens. How convenient it would be if I could tell Siri to handle those tasks for me.

“Siri, search for the 512GB 2026 iPad mini on Amazon and add it to my shopping cart.”

“Siri, review my Amazon wishlist for the luggage I recently added and tell me the latest prices.”

“Siri, check the delivery status of the Alexa photo frame I just ordered on Amazon.”

Right now, Siri can’t do any of those things. But if Siri AI and App intents are fully integrated with Amazon, I may just be able to accomplish those tasks in the future.

IMDB is my go-to app for getting info on movies, TV shows, performers, directors, and more. After I open the app and run a search, I often want specific details, such as the rating and runtime of a particular film or TV episode.

Also: AI completely changed how I develop iPhone apps

To simplify that process, I’ve love to be able to ask Siri: “Siri, search IMDB for the 1935 movie ‘The Bride of Frankenstein,’ give me the running time, tell me where I can stream it, and add it to my watchlist.” If Siri could accomplish all that at some point, it would get a round of applause from me.

I borrow and read a lot of e-books through my local library systems, and I use the handy Libby app for that. Here, I can search different libraries for books by title, author, or subject. I can then borrow a book and read it through the Libby app or, more typically, through the Amazon Kindle app. For this, I have to manually open the app and search among the various libraries for the book I want.

Also: I lost 100 pounds in 7 months: How a smart scale and Apple Watch helped

Instead, I’d like to ask Siri to do that for me. I might say: “Siri, look in Libby for books about Alan Turing, give me the titles of the ones you find, and tell me which ones are currently available to borrow.”

My wife and I are big theater buffs, and we see a lot of plays on Broadway when we’re in New York and on the West End when we’re in London. Often, I buy tickets through the TodayTix service and app. For this, I’ll open the app, set the location to New York or London, look for a specific play, and then try to find seats for a certain day and time.

If TodayTix is ever fully supported by Siri AI and App Intents, I might be able to ask Siri to track down the right seats for me. I could say: “Siri, look for the play ‘Rent’ in London, give me the available performances for Dec. 5 through 9, and let me know which seats are accessible in the first 10 rows.”

As my wife and I often travel and dine out, Yelp is another app I frequently use. Here, I also have to manually launch the app and run searches for restaurants and other places. I then have to try to filter or sort the results based on location, price, and ratings.

Also: 3 handy iPhone features that make my life easier – even doing laundry

Asking Siri to tackle those tasks would certainly be a time saver. I could ask it to “find the closest Italian restaurants using Yelp and show me ones within a one-mile radius that have earned four stars or higher.”

With App Intents, Siri AI can already handle advanced, complex, multi-step tasks for built-in apps. With all developers now able to take advantage of this same support, I’m expecting a lot of apps to jump on board. Let’s hope my favorites end up on the list.

#3136. Half of New Games on Steam Are Now Made With AI. How Does This Reflect the Gaming Industry?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Most of those games are unpopular, with 10 or fewer reviews from gamers.

Steam, the digital marketplace for PC games from game studio Valve, has hit a major milestone, sparking pushback from parts of the gaming community: Approximately 50% of new Steam games in October were made with the help of AI.

This underscores a growing trend in gaming, where more games are made with some form of AI assistance — specifically, generative AI, which developers have used to generate code, art assets, voice lines and more. Developers are adopting the technology in increasing numbers.

The numbers come from a Reddit user who goes by Ploz, and who used Steam’s publicly available data to see how many newly released games relied on AI in some capacity. This was possible because of Valve’s AI disclosure policy for newly released games, which requires developers to state whether they used AI in making their game. The disclosure is part of the storefront’s publicly accessible records, allowing anyone to view it.

A Valve representative did not respond to a request for comment.

The data is a snapshot of the tidal wave of AI-made games flooding storefronts, most prominently Steam. But crucially, Valve has chosen not to limit this flood, washing its hands of the problem and leaving gamers to fend for themselves in finding quality games. Developers had already been struggling to get their games noticed, and Valve’s limited curation seems completely unprepared for the firehose of AI-made games churned out on an increasing scale.

Valve implemented the AI disclosure policy in January 2024 to increase developer transparency. At the time, only 1.4% of newly released games used AI. This increased to 13.4% by the end of 2024, then to 24% by the end of 2025. It now sits at 49.9%.

There are some caveats. The AI disclosure is only required for games that use AI to create player-facing content, such as artwork, sound, character dialogue and localization. The 49.9% figure is specific to these types of games and doesn’t account for developers who use AI for behind-the-scenes tasks such as coding and bug fixes. A Google Cloud survey conducted in August 2025 showed that 87% of developers use AI for backend work, which doesn’t require disclosure on Steam.

So it’s likely that the number of games on Steam built with AI assistance is greater than 50%. Ploz notes that the only way users can avoid AI-generated games is to manually check for AI disclosures.

According to Ploz, the most common use of AI in game development is for artwork, which was mentioned in 63% of disclosures. Text and translations gobbled up 30%, while music (21%), code (16%) and voices (7%) rounded out the list. Many developers had more than one of those areas named in their disclosure, and about a quarter of developers said they were using AI for their Steam store pages and marketing.

About 3% of developers used AI directly as a game mechanic. One such example is a driving simulator called Teach My Little Sister How to Drive. Developers use AI in the game to interpret a player’s voice commands and generate the sister’s responses. To keep a playable demo of the game available to the public, the development team, Easy Fox, is paying $1,000 every day just to cover these AI operating costs — an expense so high that it was forced to take out a loan simply to keep the demo running.

For development, there are loads of options. The Unity 6 engine came out in October 2024 and includes AI code assistance, AI asset generation and third-party integration with Claude Code, Gemini and Grok. Anthropic’s Claude is a fairly popular option among smaller developers, since it supports the ability to vibe code whole games, with ChatGPT, Gemini and GitHub Copilot as other options.

Many of the games being released with the AI disclosure on Steam can be classified as slop — a derogatory term gamers have applied liberally to titles that heavily lean on generative AI for development and look derivative of other popular games. According to Ploz, most AI-enabled games are small: Around 47% of new games with fewer than 10 reviews have an AI disclosure. Among developers who released more than 10 games in a year, 68% of those games included the disclosure.

Games with AI disclosures received fewer positive reviews on average than those without. And among all newly released games with more than 1,000 reviews, only 17% include an AI disclosure. That means gamers are still gravitating toward games without an AI disclosure and pushing back against games that use the technology.

Developers seem aware of this. CNET reached out to two dozen well-known developers, including Epic Games, EA, Activision Blizzard, Ubisoft, PlayStation Studios and many others. All of them declined to comment.

Bigger studios may be using AI in their development, but it’s hard to tell the scale. There’s no such thing as an AI audit yet, and the industry seems to be relying on voluntary disclosure for now. Steam’s disclosure policy has outed smaller developers who are either worried about violating the policy and being taken off the digital storefront, or aren’t worried about the negative effects of disclosure.

A lot of dominoes had to fall for this to happen. The availability of AI tools and the increasing ease of use are definite contributors. Subreddits like r/AIGameDev have plenty of examples of people putting together games with just a few days or weeks of vibe coding, which is a lot shorter than the standard video game development cycle, which can stretch over years depending on the scale, production level and graphics quality. This practice has exploded over the last couple of years, resulting in a lot of games getting launched that are made mostly or entirely with AI.

Many of these games end up on Steam, which doesn’t have a policy limiting AI-developed games.

“Digital storefronts like Steam have already struggled to moderate low-effort and poor-quality games, as well as copycats stealing other games’ ideas,” said CNET Managing Editor David Lumb.

Valve openly admits its role in this, stating that the problem definitely exists but that the company doesn’t “want to be gatekeepers telling developers which tools they should or shouldn’t use.”

It takes a similar stance on AI cloning, with Valve’s Tom Giardino telling developers that “you must continue to grow your game by adding features, personality and creativity that stem from your own perspective as a developer.”

These policies essentially allow any AI-developed game or clone to reach the Valve storefront without pushback, which certainly contributes to the flood of newly released games with some form of player-facing AI involvement in their development.

Rival store Epic Games has a similar stance, allowing basically any game that wants to be there. The company declined to comment further about this, but CEO Tom Sweeney is an avid supporter of AI in video game development, stating that it was “perfectly logical” for developers to rely on AI to handle the mundane grunt work that takes up most of a developer’s time.

While Steam and Epic Games tend to take a more lax attitude toward AI slop, other storefronts like Itch.io are not. Itch.io has a whole policy against AI slop and the company has willingly, and at times gleefully, deleted terabytes of AI slop from its storefront. It also requires developers to disclose if they used AI but takes a much more consumer-friendly approach by letting users filter those out of search results if they don’t want to see them.

Some measures are being taken to address the proliferation of AI slop, but none will entirely stop the problem. Cloning has been a problem for many years. Mobile gamers of a certain vintage may remember the flock of Flappy Bird clones that appeared on app stores after the original game went down, and those weren’t even made with AI.

AI makes cloning much easier and faster, and some AI companies are addressing it. Anthropic recently changed Claude Opus 5.5 to prevent it from generating copies of existing games. Anthropic engineering leader Addy Osmani posted on X that using Claude to copy games infringes on intellectual property rights and violates Anthropic’s policy.

However, during CNET’s testing, we found we could still make games resembling popular titles, so cloning remains possible with a little creativity.

“This has come up over and over on the subreddit r/GameDev, and there’s no real solution if Steam and other digital storefronts don’t stem the flood of low-quality AI games drowning out the labors of love that entertain and innovate,” Lumb said.

Many developers openly oppose AI and refuse to use it in their own work. However, as the Steam stats show, that crowd’s output appears to be getting smaller and smaller every year amid the unending stream of AI games.

#3135. Reddit launches AI-powered Reviews feature – with 10,000 products to start

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Reddit is adding AI-generated product reviews that compile real user sentiment from across communities. Here's how they work.

If you regularly turn to Reddit for product advice, your experience is about to change.

Reddit announced a new feature on Tuesday called Reddit Reviews, which takes conversations from subreddits across the site and compiles them into AI-generated, in-depth product summaries. The feature works much like Google AI Overviews and is likely an attempt to better compete with them.

When you search for a product on Reddit, you’ll see an “easy-to-digest format” that has a “what people are saying” recap. A visual breakdown will show whether conversations are generally positive, mixed, or negative, as well as common sentiments among users. If you want to go deeper, Reddit says you can browse comments about a product, apply topic filters, read original user discussions, ask follow-up questions, or explore other commonly compared products.

In an example shared by Reddit, a user searches for “Best headphones 2026.” The search returns several results with tags like “Very positive,” “Positive,” and “Mixed.” Clicking on one expands to a review that says, “Reddit likes the XL224’s fantastic battery life, powerful bass, and strong sound quality, while the steep price and fit on smaller heads draws criticism.”

“A mix of generative AI and other in-house technology” is used to identify themes and summarize what people are saying, a representative explained, and added that “the technologies and models we use may evolve over time to best support the experience.”

Perhaps the most important part is that Reddit Reviews are shaped by users, and companies can’t pay to have product features. For a community sensitive to commercialization, this is a big deal.

My first concern was about bots or other fake reviews, but a Reddit representative said they’re taking that into consideration. “Platform-wide,” the representative said, “we are labeling apps and prompting accounts we detect to be running automations to either verify there’s a human behind the username or be labeled as an app.” In this context, an app is a registered API client that’s developed to interact with Reddit (including posting, commenting, upvoting, and scraping). In short, the system will label known bots.

Also: Ring’s new drone patrols your home to keep watch – even upstairsSpecifically for reviews, a “review conversation” will appear that describes a person’s experience with a product. Reddit also has “defined rules,” it says, “to help our LLMs identify these review conversations based on the surrounding conversation for context.”

You’ll start to see Reddit Reviews over the next few weeks in the US on iOS, Android, and browser versions of the site. Around 10,000 products across electronics, health and beauty, home and garden, and fashion and apparel will be available to start.

I find myself frequently adding “reddit” to Google searches for everything from the best restaurants in a city to the best headphones for my kids, so these overviews are definitely intriguing. It’s not easy right now to wade through numerous threads, so if this does make it easier to get true user sentiment, it could be a big plus.
